visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Students can resize a cell and watch volume outpace surface area. This makes the limit on cell size intuitive instead of abstract.

visualization_candidates.concept: Generalized prokaryotic cell structure (nucleoid, ribosomes, cell wall, capsule, flagella, pili)
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Exploring the layers and appendages in 3D shows how the capsule, cell wall, and plasma membrane are arranged around the nucleoid.

visualization_candidates.concept: Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cell size and compartmentalization
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: A side-by-side scaled comparison highlights both the size difference and the presence of membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotes.

summary: Motion is relative: a description of motion is only meaningful when a reference frame (the coordinate system used to describe positions) is specified.
Distance is the total length of the path traveled. Displacement (Δd = d_f − d₀) is the net change in position, so a round trip has a nonzero distance but zero displacement.
Scalars (distance, speed) have magnitude only. Vectors (displacement) have both magnitude and direction.
To calculate in one dimension, choose an origin and a positive direction, measure positions consistently, and use the signs to find displacement. Distance simply adds the path lengths.
Convert all quantities to SI units, such as meters and seconds, before calculating, as the Mars Climate Orbiter loss shows.

sections.title: Kinematics, Position, and Reference Frames
sections.body_markdown:
Physics often begins with **kinematics**, the study of motion *without* considering its causes. Motion is everywhere: a tennis game, a space probe flying past Neptune, blood moving through your veins, and even atoms in inanimate objects.

How do you know something is moving? First you need its **position**, which is the location of an object at a particular time. Position must be specified **relative to a convenient reference frame**.

A **reference frame** is the coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described.

- **Earth** is often used as a reference frame. For example, a rocket launch is described by the rocket's position relative to Earth as a whole.
- A smaller stationary frame also works. A professor's position can be described relative to the nearby whiteboard.
- Some reference frames are themselves moving relative to Earth. To describe a person's position inside an airplane, we use the **airplane**, not Earth, as the reference frame.

You can only know how fast and in what direction an object's position is changing against a background of something else. That background must either be not moving or be moving with a known speed and direction.

sections.title: Motion Is Relative
sections.body_markdown:
Your **classroom** can be a reference frame. Because the walls are not moving, you can measure your walk to the door against them. The classroom also lets you see *that* other things move, such as classmates entering or a book falling. It lets you tell their *direction* too, as in “The teacher is moving toward the door.”

**You** can also be a reference frame:

- If you stay seated while classmates leave, you see them moving away from you.
- If you leave together with them, you are moving in the same direction, so your view of their motion changes.

**Example: a bouncing basketball.** Picture a partner bouncing a ball while walking forward.

- If you stand still, you see the ball move forward as it bounces.
- If you walk alongside your partner, your description of the ball's motion is different.

The ball's motion *depends* on the reference frame, and it looks different in different frames.

**Galileo's ship.** Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was one of the first scientists to explore this idea. He imagined a windowless ship moving at constant speed and direction on a perfectly calm sea. He concluded the following:

- Only by looking at each other can a person on the ship and a person on shore describe the motion of one relative to the other.
- Their descriptions are symmetric, or opposite. The person on the ship sees the person on land moving past. The person on shore sees the ship moving past.
- Observers moving at a constant speed and direction relative to each other describe motion in the same way.

The conclusion is that a description of motion is only meaningful if you specify a reference frame.

This is also why riders on a very fast train, such as the Shanghai Maglev at close to 300 mph, may not notice they are moving unless they look out the window.

sections.title: Distance vs. Displacement
sections.body_markdown:
Physicists use **d** for position.

- **d₀** (said “d naught”) is the initial position.
- **d_f** is the final position.
- Some books use x or s instead of d.

**Distance** is the length of the path between an object's initial position and its final position. Distance depends on the path taken. Driving to a friend's house is probably longer than the straight line between the two houses.

**Displacement** is the net change in position of an object, written **Δd**. The Greek letter delta (Δ) means “change in.”

**Round-trip example.** Suppose school is a 5 km straight drive from home.

- **One way to school:** the distance is 5 km and the displacement is 5 km. They are the same because the route is a straight line in one direction.
- **Round trip (home → school → home):** the total distance is 10 km. The car ends where it started, so the displacement is **0**.

Why is the displacement zero? Call the direction toward school positive (+) and the opposite direction negative (–). Then the +5 km and –5 km cancel when added together.

**Another example: one lap of an oval race track.**

- The distance is the perimeter of the track.
- The magnitude of displacement is the shortest distance between the start line and the finish line.

In short, distance describes the **total path** traveled. Displacement describes the **shortest path** between the starting and ending points.

sections.title: Scalars and Vectors
sections.body_markdown:
**Magnitude** means the size or amount of a quantity: how big or how much.

A **scalar** has magnitude, and sometimes a sign, but does **not** take direction into account.

- Distance
- Speed
- Electric charge
- Temperature in Celsius

A **vector** has **both magnitude and direction**.

- Displacement

A vector with magnitude zero is a special case that has no direction.

**Writing convention:** vectors are written in bold or with an arrow above the variable, while scalars are written in italics.

**Quick check: is it a scalar or a vector?**

- *“I drove 10 km.”* Only a size is given, so this is a scalar (distance).
- *“I ended up 1 km west of where I started.”* A size and a direction are given, so this is a vector (displacement).

sections.title: Calculating Displacement and Distance in One Dimension
sections.body_markdown:
Find displacement by subtracting the initial position from the final position:

**Δd = d_f − d₀**

If the final position equals the initial position, then Δd = 0.

**Set up your axis first:**

1. Choose an **origin (O)**, the zero point.
2. Choose which direction is **positive**. The opposite direction is negative.
3. Measure all positions consistently from that zero.

You may place the origin wherever you like, so choose the easiest axis, direction, and zero. In the drive-to-school example, home is placed at zero and school is in the positive direction. For the one-way trip, d₀ = 0 km and d_f = 5 km, so Δd = 5 km.

**Worked example.** A cyclist rides 3 km west, then turns around and rides 2 km east. Take east as positive and west as negative.

- Final position: −3 km + 2 km = −1 km. She started at the origin, so her **displacement = −1 km**, which can also be stated as 1 km west.
- **Distance** = 3 km + 2 km = **5 km**. Direction does not matter for distance.
- **Magnitude of displacement** = 1 km.

The same method works for north–south (y-direction) motion.

**Practice 1.** Right-to-left is positive. A student walks 32 m right, then 17 m left.

- Displacement = −32 m + 17 m = **−15 m**
- Distance = 32 m + 17 m = **49 m**

**Practice 2.** Tiana's original direction is positive. She jogs 1.5 km, then 2.4 km back, then 0.7 km in the original direction.

- Displacement = 1.5 − 2.4 + 0.7 = **−0.2 km**
- Distance = 1.5 + 2.4 + 0.7 = **4.6 km**

Notice that distance is never negative, but displacement can be.

sections.title: Using SI Units
sections.body_markdown:
Physicists use standard units so that results are easier to compare. These standard units are called **SI units** (International System of Units), and they are based on the metric system.

- The SI unit for displacement and distance is the **meter (m)**.
- The SI unit of time is the **second (s)**.

Problems sometimes give kilometers, miles, feet, or other units. If one quantity is in SI units and another is not, **convert all quantities to the same system before calculating**.

**Why it matters: the Mars Climate Orbiter.** In 1998, NASA launched this $125-million satellite to monitor the Martian atmosphere. Scientists made calculations in English units (feet, inches, pounds) and forgot to convert them to SI units. Instead of orbiting Mars, the probe flew into the Martian atmosphere and disintegrated.

**Conversion example.** At one point the orbiter was 187,000 feet above the surface. Use 1 m = 3.281 ft.

- 187,000 ft ÷ 3.281 ft/m ≈ 57,000 m
- 57,000 m ≈ **57 km**

visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Switching the camera between frames lets students directly see that the same ball or ship traces different paths depending on the observer, which is hard to picture from text alone.

visualization_candidates.concept: Distance vs. displacement along a one-dimensional axis with an adjustable origin and positive direction (e.g., the cyclist going 3 km west and 2 km east)
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Animating the motion step by step, with a running distance counter beside the displacement arrow, shows why distance accumulates while displacement can shrink, change sign, or return to zero.

summary: A description of motion depends on the reference frame, and there is no single correct frame.
Distance (a scalar) is the length of the path traveled, while displacement (a vector) is the change in position; a round trip has zero displacement but nonzero distance.
Average speed is distance divided by time, average velocity is displacement divided by time, and the magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals instantaneous speed.
The slope of a position vs. time graph is velocity; for a curve, use the slope of the tangent line to get instantaneous velocity.
The slope of a velocity vs. time graph is acceleration, and the area under it is displacement.
Real-world planning combines map-scale measurements with distance, speed, and time relationships.

sections.title: Key Terms of One-Dimensional Kinematics
sections.body_markdown:
**Kinematics** is the study of motion without considering its causes. To describe motion, we need a shared vocabulary.

- **Reference frame:** a coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described. A description of motion *depends on* the reference frame, so you should always specify one.
- **Position:** the location of an object at any particular time.
- **Magnitude:** size or amount.
- **Scalar:** a quantity that has magnitude (and possibly sign) but no direction. Examples are distance and speed.
- **Vector:** a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Examples are displacement and velocity.
- **Instantaneous speed:** speed at a specific instant in time.
- **Instantaneous velocity:** velocity at a specific instant in time.
- **Acceleration:** the rate at which velocity changes.

**Reference frames in action**

Suppose you drive east past a friend standing at a bus stop. In your friend's frame, you are moving. In your frame, your friend is moving toward the west.

There is no single "correct" reference frame, because motion is relative. For example, a passenger on a moving train throws a ball straight up:

- A fellow passenger sees only vertical motion.
- An observer on the platform sees both vertical and horizontal motion.

sections.title: Distance vs. Displacement
sections.body_markdown:
- **Distance** is the length of the path actually traveled between an initial and a final position. It is a scalar.
- **Displacement** is the change in position of an object against a fixed axis. It is a vector, so it has magnitude and direction.

A car's **odometer** records distance, not displacement.

**Example 1: biker.** A biker rides 50 miles west, then 80 miles east.

- Distance = 50 + 80 = 130 miles.
- Displacement = 30 miles east.

**Example 2: round trips.** When an object returns to its starting point, its displacement is zero but its distance is not.

- A space shuttle that orbits Earth once travels a distance equal to the circumference of the orbit, but its displacement is zero.
- A bowling ball that rolls down the lane and is returned to the holder has zero displacement. Its distance is twice the lane length.

**Example 3: bouncing ball.** A ball is dropped from 1 m. It bounces to 0.8 m, then 0.5 m, then 0.2 m. Up is positive.

- Distance = 1 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 4 m.
- Displacement = –1 m, because the ball ends 1 m below where it started.

sections.title: Speed and Velocity
sections.body_markdown:
- **Speed** is the rate at which an object changes its location.
- **Average speed** = distance traveled ÷ time during which the motion occurs. It is a scalar.
- **Velocity** is the speed *and* direction of an object. It is a vector.
- **Average velocity** = displacement ÷ time over which the displacement occurs.

**How the quantities relate**

- The magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals the instantaneous speed.
- A speedometer shows speed but not direction. So it alone cannot give instantaneous velocity.
- If velocity is constant, average velocity and instantaneous velocity are the same.
- For a car moving at constant speed in one direction on a straight road, the magnitude of average velocity equals the average speed.

**Zero velocity with nonzero speed**

A swimmer completes 3 laps in 9 minutes, where one lap is across the pool and back. The swimmer's average velocity is zero because the total displacement is zero, even though the average speed is not zero.

sections.title: Solving Multi-Step Problems
sections.body_markdown:
Use this strategy:

1. Choose a positive direction.
2. Decide whether the question asks for a scalar (distance or speed) or a vector (displacement or velocity).
3. Convert units so they match.
4. Apply the definitions.

**Unit conversion.** A car moves at 86.4 km/h. How far does it travel in 3.3 s?

- Convert: 86.4 km/h = 24 m/s.
- Distance = 24 m/s × 3.3 s ≈ 79.2 m.

**Comparing average speeds.** Four cyclists travel these distances:

- Cyclist 1: 95 m in 27 s ≈ 3.5 m/s
- Cyclist 2: 87 m in 22 s ≈ 4.0 m/s
- Cyclist 3: 106 m in 26 s ≈ 4.1 m/s
- Cyclist 4: 108 m in 24 s = 4.5 m/s

Cyclist 4 has the greatest average speed.

**Limits on displacement.** A car averages 23 m/s for 82 s, so it travels about 1,886 m. Its displacement cannot be larger than its distance. A displacement of 2,000 m is therefore impossible.

**Same path, different speed.** A trip takes time t at average speed v. Returning along the same path at 3v takes t/3.

**Different paths, same endpoints.** A father walks straight to a bus stop 75 m away at 2.2 m/s. His daughter runs a varied path at 3.5 m/s, and they arrive at the same time.

- Time = 75 ÷ 2.2 ≈ 34 s.
- Daughter's distance ≈ 3.5 × 34 ≈ 119 m.
- In a straight line, she would have gone about 44 m beyond the stop.

**Round trip.** Alan walks 1.3 km east, 0.68 km east, 1.1 km north, and 0.42 km north, then returns home along the same path.

- Distance = 2 × 3.5 km = 7 km.
- Displacement = 0 km.

sections.title: Interpreting Position vs. Time Graphs
sections.body_markdown:
On a motion graph, the **independent variable** (usually time) goes on the horizontal axis. The **dependent variable** changes as the independent variable changes.

**Reading a position vs. time graph**

- The **slope** of a position vs. time graph is the velocity.
- For a straight-line graph, the slope is the average velocity.
- For a curved graph, find instantaneous velocity by drawing the **tangent** line at that point and taking its slope. A tangent is a line that touches the curve at exactly one point.

**Example: a train trip.** A train speeds up from rest for 15 min, cruises at 100 miles/hour for half an hour, then slows to a stop over 15 min. Its position graph has three parts:

- A concave-upward curve while speeding up.
- A straight line with slope 100 miles/hour while cruising.
- A concave-downward curve while slowing.

**Example: a hockey puck.** A puck travels 20 m out at constant speed, then is sent straight back. Its graph is a downward-opening V. The net displacement is 0 m, so the average velocity is 0 m/s, even though the distance is 40 m.

sections.title: Interpreting Velocity vs. Time Graphs
sections.body_markdown:
**Reading a velocity vs. time graph**

- The **slope** is the acceleration.
- The **area under the curve** is the displacement.
- Average velocity can be found by taking the weighted average of all the velocities.

**Example.** A car moving at 10 m/s doubles its velocity 10 s later. The area under its velocity graph gives the car's displacement during those 10 s.

**Estimating displacement from a curved graph**

- Divide the graph into sections.
- Find the area of each section.
- Add the areas together.

Using more divisions follows the curve more closely. In one review problem, seven divisions and two divisions gave different estimates of displacement (14,312.5 m vs. 15,500 m).

**Data needed for acceleration.** To estimate average acceleration from position measurements, you need at least three data points.

sections.title: Applying Kinematics to a Real-World Map Task
sections.body_markdown:
The chapter's performance task asks you to plan logistics for a concert on the National Mall in Washington, DC. You use a map scale to measure the distances you need.

**Part 1: Wire lengths**

Long-distance speakers can project sound up to 0.35 miles. They must be wired to a power supply in the concert area.

1. Trace the allowed path for the wire. Wire cannot go over buildings or memorials, and in one case it cannot cross water.
2. Measure the path on the map and convert it with the scale.
3. The speaker only needs to get within 0.35 miles of the target. Use this to find the *minimum* wire length.

**Part 2: Motorcade speed**

The motorcade travels a route along streets: west on E Street, then south on 23rd Street.

1. Measure each leg of the route and add them to get the total distance in miles.
2. Convert 5 minutes to hours: 5/60 h.
3. Minimum speed = distance ÷ time.

**Part 3: Helicopter time**

The helicopter flies directly from one landing zone to the other.

1. Measure the straight-line distance between the landing zones.
2. Time = distance ÷ 30 mph.
3. Convert the result to minutes.

**Key insight:** the motorcade's path length (a distance) is longer than the helicopter's straight-line path, which matches the size of the displacement.

summary: Cells are the smallest units of life; specialized cells work together to form tissues, organs, organ systems, and whole organisms.
Magnification enlarges an image, while resolving power determines how clearly two nearby structures can be told apart.
Light microscopes (up to ~400×, or ~1,000× with oil immersion) can view living cells but need thin samples and often stains; dissecting microscopes (20–80×) give upright, 3D views of thick objects.
Electron microscopes give higher magnification and resolution but require killed specimens in a vacuum; SEM shows surfaces by reflection, TEM shows internal structures.

Hooke named the cell, van Leeuwenhoek observed animalcules, bacteria, and protozoa, and Schleiden and Schwann proposed the unified cell theory: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells.

sections.title: Cells: The Building Blocks of Organisms
sections.body_markdown:
Picture a brick wall: its basic building block is a single brick. In the same way, the basic building blocks of your body are **cells**. A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing, and a living thing is called an **organism**.

Your body contains many kinds of cells, each specialized for a specific purpose. They work together like the different materials in a house:

- **Epithelial cells** protect the surface of the body and cover the organs and body cavities.
- **Bone cells** help support and protect the body.
- **Immune system cells** fight invading bacteria.
- **Red blood cells** carry oxygen throughout the body.

Each type plays a vital role in growth, development, and day-to-day maintenance of the body. Despite their enormous variety, all cells share certain fundamental characteristics.

sections.title: Levels of Organization: How Parts Work Together
sections.body_markdown:
In multicellular organisms, cells do not work alone. Each level builds on the one below it:

1. **Cells** of one particular kind interconnect and perform shared functions to form a **tissue** (for example, muscle, connective, or nervous tissue).
2. Several tissues combine to form an **organ** (for example, the stomach, heart, or brain).
3. Several organs make up an **organ system** (such as the digestive, circulatory, or nervous system).
4. Several systems functioning together form an **organism** (such as an elephant).

The key idea is cooperation: each level depends on the coordinated work of the parts beneath it.

All cells fall into one of two broad categories. Animal, plant, fungal, and protist cells are **eukaryotic**, while bacteria and archaea are **prokaryotic**.

sections.title: Microscopy Basics: Magnification and Resolving Power
sections.body_markdown:
With few exceptions, cells are too small to see with the naked eye. A **microscope** is an instrument that magnifies an object, and images of cells taken with a microscope are called **micrographs**.

For scale: a typical human red blood cell is about 8 micrometers (µm) across, while the head of a pin is about 2 millimeters across, so roughly 250 red blood cells could fit on a pinhead.

Two parameters work together to make a useful image:

- **Magnification**: the degree of enlargement of an object.
- **Resolving power**: the ability of a microscope to let the eye distinguish two adjacent structures as separate. The higher the resolution, the closer two objects can be while still appearing separate, and the better the clarity and detail.

Enlarging an image is only helpful if the detail is also clear, which is why both matter.

sections.title: Light and Dissecting Microscopes
sections.body_markdown:
### Light microscopes
Most student microscopes are light microscopes. Visible light passes through and is bent by the lens system. Because light enters the specimen from below and is focused onto the observer's eye, the sample must be **thin or translucent**.

- Magnify up to about **400×** in typical college labs; **oil immersion lenses** raise this to about **1,000×** for smaller cells like most prokaryotes.
- Good for viewing **living organisms**, but cells are generally transparent, so their parts are hard to see unless **stained**, and staining usually kills the cells.
- Two sets of lenses produce an **inverted image**: a specimen appears upside-down and reversed, and moving the slide left makes it appear to move right.

### Dissecting microscopes
- Lower magnification (**20 to 80×**) but give a **three-dimensional view**.
- Thick objects can be examined with many components in focus at once, showing tissue structure and whole-organism anatomy.
- **Binocular**: two separate lens systems, one per eye, set apart to give a sense of depth that makes hand manipulations easier.
- Extra optics correct the image so it appears **upright**, as if seen by the naked eye.
- Light usually comes from **above** the sample, but may also come from below.

sections.title: Electron Microscopes: Scanning vs. Transmission
sections.body_markdown:
**Electron microscopes** use a beam of electrons instead of light. This gives higher magnification, more detail, and higher resolving power.

The trade-offs:

- Specimen preparation kills the sample, so **live cells cannot be viewed**.
- The electron beam moves best in a **vacuum**, which also makes viewing living material impossible.
- They are significantly more **bulky and expensive** than light microscopes.

### Two types
| Feature | Scanning (SEM) | Transmission (TEM) |
|---|---|---|
| How the beam works | Moves back and forth across the cell's surface | Passes through the cell |
| What you see | Surface details, by reflection | Internal structures |
| Preparation note | Usually coated with a metal like gold | — |

For example, a scanning electron micrograph can show Salmonella bacteria invading human cells in far more detail than a light microscope image of the same bacteria.

sections.title: Microscopy in Practice: The Cytotechnologist
sections.body_markdown:
**Cytotechnologists** (cyto- = cell) study cells through microscopic examination and other lab tests. In a **Pap smear**, cells from the uterine cervix are sent to a lab, where a cytotechnologist stains them and looks for changes that could indicate cervical cancer or a microbial infection.

They decide which cellular changes are normal or abnormal and study specimens from all organs. When they find abnormalities, they consult a **pathologist**, a medical doctor who makes the clinical diagnosis. Early detection lets treatment begin sooner, which usually improves the chances of success.

sections.title: The Unified Cell Theory and Its Pioneers
sections.body_markdown:
Our understanding of cells grew as lenses improved:

- **Robert Hooke (1665)**: In *Micrographia*, he coined the term **cell** (from Latin *cella*, "small room") for the box-like structures he saw in cork tissue.
- **Antony van Leeuwenhoek (1600s–1670s)**: A Dutch shopkeeper skilled at crafting lenses, he observed moving protists and sperm, which he called **"animalcules,"** and in the 1670s discovered bacteria and protozoa.
- Later advances in lenses and microscope construction let scientists see components inside cells.
- **Matthias Schleiden** (botanist) and **Theodor Schwann** (zoologist), studying tissues in the late 1830s, proposed the **unified cell theory**.

### The unified cell theory
1. All living things are composed of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of life.
3. All new cells arise from existing cells.

These principles still stand today.

summary: Prokaryotes include Bacteria and Archaea; eukaryotes include animals, plants, fungi, and protists.
All cells share four components: a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes.
Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is in the nucleoid, and bacteria have a peptidoglycan cell wall.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles with specialized functions.
Prokaryotes are 0.1–5.0 µm in diameter, while eukaryotic cells are 10–100 µm.
Cell size is limited because volume grows faster than surface area, so a larger cell has less surface relative to its contents for transporting materials.

sections.title: Two Broad Categories of Cells
sections.body_markdown:
Every cell falls into one of two broad categories: **prokaryotic** or **eukaryotic**.

- **Prokaryotes** are the predominantly single-celled organisms of the domains **Bacteria** and **Archaea**. The name comes from *pro-* (before) and *-karyon-* (nucleus).
- **Eukaryotes** include **animal cells, plant cells, fungi, and protists**. The prefix *eu-* means "true."

This grouping builds on the **unified cell theory**, proposed by Schleiden and Schwann in the late 1830s. It has three principles:

1. All living things are composed of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of life.
3. All new cells arise from existing cells.

sections.title: Four Components Shared by All Cells
sections.body_markdown:
Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ in many ways, but all cells share four common components:

1. **Plasma membrane**: an outer covering that separates the cell's interior from its surrounding environment.
2. **Cytoplasm**: a jelly-like region inside the cell where the other cellular components are found.
3. **DNA**: the genetic material of the cell.
4. **Ribosomes**: particles that synthesize proteins.

sections.title: Structure of Prokaryotic Cells
sections.body_markdown:
A prokaryotic cell is a simple, single-celled (unicellular) organism. It has **no nucleus and no other membrane-bound organelles**. Its DNA sits in a darkened central region called the **nucleoid**.

Bacteria have some extra outer structures:

- **Cell wall**: made of **peptidoglycan**, which is composed of sugars and amino acids. Unlike Archaea and eukaryotes, bacteria have this type of wall. It adds protection, helps the cell keep its shape, and prevents dehydration.
- **Capsule**: many bacteria have a polysaccharide capsule that lets the cell attach to surfaces in its environment.

Some prokaryotes also have surface appendages:

- **Flagella** are used for locomotion.
- **Pili**: most are used to exchange genetic material during a type of reproduction called **conjugation**.
- **Fimbriae** are another type of surface appendage some prokaryotes have.

sections.title: Structure of Eukaryotic Cells
sections.body_markdown:
A eukaryotic cell has a **membrane-bound nucleus**. It also has other membrane-bound compartments, called **organelles**, each with a specialized function.

- *Eukaryotic* means "true kernel" or "true nucleus," which refers to the membrane-bound nucleus.
- *Organelle* means "little organ." Organelles do specialized jobs in the cell, much as your body's organs do specialized jobs in your body.

Eukaryotic cells are more complex than prokaryotic cells. Their organelles allow different functions to happen in the cell at the same time.

Cells also show the principle that **form follows function**: you can often deduce what a structure does by looking at its shape. Birds and fish are an example at the level of whole organisms. Their streamlined bodies let them move quickly through air or water.

sections.title: Comparing Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes
sections.body_markdown:
**Similarities**

- Both have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes.

**Differences**

| Feature | Prokaryotic cells | Eukaryotic cells |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Absent; DNA is in the nucleoid | Membrane-bound nucleus |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present, with specialized functions |
| Organisms | Bacteria and Archaea | Animals, plants, fungi, protists |
| Diameter | 0.1–5.0 µm | 10–100 µm |
| Complexity | Simple, unicellular | More complex structure |

sections.title: Cell Size and the Surface Area to Volume Relationship
sections.body_markdown:
Prokaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm in diameter, which is much smaller than eukaryotic cells at 10–100 µm.

**Why small size helps prokaryotes**

- Ions and organic molecules that enter the cell spread quickly to other parts of it.
- Wastes produced inside the cell can quickly move out.

**Why cell size is limited**

- As a cell grows, its **volume increases much more quickly than its surface area**.
- Materials must be transported across the cell's surface. So as the cell gets larger, its surface becomes relatively smaller compared with its contents.
- This makes it harder and harder for the cell to take in enough materials to support the processes inside it.

**How eukaryotes cope**

Larger eukaryotic cells have evolved structural adaptations that improve transport within the cell. Without these adaptations, their large size would not be possible.

visualization_candidates.concept: Surface area to volume ratio as a cell grows
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Students can resize a cell and watch volume outpace surface area. This makes the limit on cell size intuitive instead of abstract.

visualization_candidates.concept: Generalized prokaryotic cell structure (nucleoid, ribosomes, cell wall, capsule, flagella, pili)
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Exploring the layers and appendages in 3D shows how the capsule, cell wall, and plasma membrane are arranged around the nucleoid.

visualization_candidates.concept: Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cell size and compartmentalization
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: A side-by-side scaled comparison highlights both the size difference and the presence of membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotes.

summary: Motion is relative: a description of motion is only meaningful when a reference frame (the coordinate system used to describe positions) is specified.
Distance is the total length of the path traveled. Displacement (Δd = d_f − d₀) is the net change in position, so a round trip has a nonzero distance but zero displacement.
Scalars (distance, speed) have magnitude only. Vectors (displacement) have both magnitude and direction.
To calculate in one dimension, choose an origin and a positive direction, measure positions consistently, and use the signs to find displacement. Distance simply adds the path lengths.
Convert all quantities to SI units, such as meters and seconds, before calculating, as the Mars Climate Orbiter loss shows.

sections.title: Kinematics, Position, and Reference Frames
sections.body_markdown:
Physics often begins with **kinematics**, the study of motion *without* considering its causes. Motion is everywhere: a tennis game, a space probe flying past Neptune, blood moving through your veins, and even atoms in inanimate objects.

How do you know something is moving? First you need its **position**, which is the location of an object at a particular time. Position must be specified **relative to a convenient reference frame**.

A **reference frame** is the coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described.

- **Earth** is often used as a reference frame. For example, a rocket launch is described by the rocket's position relative to Earth as a whole.
- A smaller stationary frame also works. A professor's position can be described relative to the nearby whiteboard.
- Some reference frames are themselves moving relative to Earth. To describe a person's position inside an airplane, we use the **airplane**, not Earth, as the reference frame.

You can only know how fast and in what direction an object's position is changing against a background of something else. That background must either be not moving or be moving with a known speed and direction.

sections.title: Motion Is Relative
sections.body_markdown:
Your **classroom** can be a reference frame. Because the walls are not moving, you can measure your walk to the door against them. The classroom also lets you see *that* other things move, such as classmates entering or a book falling. It lets you tell their *direction* too, as in “The teacher is moving toward the door.”

**You** can also be a reference frame:

- If you stay seated while classmates leave, you see them moving away from you.
- If you leave together with them, you are moving in the same direction, so your view of their motion changes.

**Example: a bouncing basketball.** Picture a partner bouncing a ball while walking forward.

- If you stand still, you see the ball move forward as it bounces.
- If you walk alongside your partner, your description of the ball's motion is different.

The ball's motion *depends* on the reference frame, and it looks different in different frames.

**Galileo's ship.** Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was one of the first scientists to explore this idea. He imagined a windowless ship moving at constant speed and direction on a perfectly calm sea. He concluded the following:

- Only by looking at each other can a person on the ship and a person on shore describe the motion of one relative to the other.
- Their descriptions are symmetric, or opposite. The person on the ship sees the person on land moving past. The person on shore sees the ship moving past.
- Observers moving at a constant speed and direction relative to each other describe motion in the same way.

The conclusion is that a description of motion is only meaningful if you specify a reference frame.

This is also why riders on a very fast train, such as the Shanghai Maglev at close to 300 mph, may not notice they are moving unless they look out the window.

sections.title: Distance vs. Displacement
sections.body_markdown:
Physicists use **d** for position.

- **d₀** (said “d naught”) is the initial position.
- **d_f** is the final position.
- Some books use x or s instead of d.

**Distance** is the length of the path between an object's initial position and its final position. Distance depends on the path taken. Driving to a friend's house is probably longer than the straight line between the two houses.

**Displacement** is the net change in position of an object, written **Δd**. The Greek letter delta (Δ) means “change in.”

**Round-trip example.** Suppose school is a 5 km straight drive from home.

- **One way to school:** the distance is 5 km and the displacement is 5 km. They are the same because the route is a straight line in one direction.
- **Round trip (home → school → home):** the total distance is 10 km. The car ends where it started, so the displacement is **0**.

Why is the displacement zero? Call the direction toward school positive (+) and the opposite direction negative (–). Then the +5 km and –5 km cancel when added together.

**Another example: one lap of an oval race track.**

- The distance is the perimeter of the track.
- The magnitude of displacement is the shortest distance between the start line and the finish line.

In short, distance describes the **total path** traveled. Displacement describes the **shortest path** between the starting and ending points.

sections.title: Scalars and Vectors
sections.body_markdown:
**Magnitude** means the size or amount of a quantity: how big or how much.

A **scalar** has magnitude, and sometimes a sign, but does **not** take direction into account.

- Distance
- Speed
- Electric charge
- Temperature in Celsius

A **vector** has **both magnitude and direction**.

- Displacement

A vector with magnitude zero is a special case that has no direction.

**Writing convention:** vectors are written in bold or with an arrow above the variable, while scalars are written in italics.

**Quick check: is it a scalar or a vector?**

- *“I drove 10 km.”* Only a size is given, so this is a scalar (distance).
- *“I ended up 1 km west of where I started.”* A size and a direction are given, so this is a vector (displacement).

sections.title: Calculating Displacement and Distance in One Dimension
sections.body_markdown:
Find displacement by subtracting the initial position from the final position:

**Δd = d_f − d₀**

If the final position equals the initial position, then Δd = 0.

**Set up your axis first:**

1. Choose an **origin (O)**, the zero point.
2. Choose which direction is **positive**. The opposite direction is negative.
3. Measure all positions consistently from that zero.

You may place the origin wherever you like, so choose the easiest axis, direction, and zero. In the drive-to-school example, home is placed at zero and school is in the positive direction. For the one-way trip, d₀ = 0 km and d_f = 5 km, so Δd = 5 km.

**Worked example.** A cyclist rides 3 km west, then turns around and rides 2 km east. Take east as positive and west as negative.

- Final position: −3 km + 2 km = −1 km. She started at the origin, so her **displacement = −1 km**, which can also be stated as 1 km west.
- **Distance** = 3 km + 2 km = **5 km**. Direction does not matter for distance.
- **Magnitude of displacement** = 1 km.

The same method works for north–south (y-direction) motion.

**Practice 1.** Right-to-left is positive. A student walks 32 m right, then 17 m left.

- Displacement = −32 m + 17 m = **−15 m**
- Distance = 32 m + 17 m = **49 m**

**Practice 2.** Tiana's original direction is positive. She jogs 1.5 km, then 2.4 km back, then 0.7 km in the original direction.

- Displacement = 1.5 − 2.4 + 0.7 = **−0.2 km**
- Distance = 1.5 + 2.4 + 0.7 = **4.6 km**

Notice that distance is never negative, but displacement can be.

sections.title: Using SI Units
sections.body_markdown:
Physicists use standard units so that results are easier to compare. These standard units are called **SI units** (International System of Units), and they are based on the metric system.

- The SI unit for displacement and distance is the **meter (m)**.
- The SI unit of time is the **second (s)**.

Problems sometimes give kilometers, miles, feet, or other units. If one quantity is in SI units and another is not, **convert all quantities to the same system before calculating**.

**Why it matters: the Mars Climate Orbiter.** In 1998, NASA launched this $125-million satellite to monitor the Martian atmosphere. Scientists made calculations in English units (feet, inches, pounds) and forgot to convert them to SI units. Instead of orbiting Mars, the probe flew into the Martian atmosphere and disintegrated.

**Conversion example.** At one point the orbiter was 187,000 feet above the surface. Use 1 m = 3.281 ft.

- 187,000 ft ÷ 3.281 ft/m ≈ 57,000 m
- 57,000 m ≈ **57 km**

visualization_candidates.concept: Same motion viewed from two reference frames (bouncing basketball seen by a stationary observer vs. an observer walking alongside, or Galileo's ship vs. shore)
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Switching the camera between frames lets students directly see that the same ball or ship traces different paths depending on the observer, which is hard to picture from text alone.

visualization_candidates.concept: Distance vs. displacement along a one-dimensional axis with an adjustable origin and positive direction (e.g., the cyclist going 3 km west and 2 km east)
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Animating the motion step by step, with a running distance counter beside the displacement arrow, shows why distance accumulates while displacement can shrink, change sign, or return to zero.

summary: A description of motion depends on the reference frame, and there is no single correct frame.
Distance (a scalar) is the length of the path traveled, while displacement (a vector) is the change in position; a round trip has zero displacement but nonzero distance.
Average speed is distance divided by time, average velocity is displacement divided by time, and the magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals instantaneous speed.
The slope of a position vs. time graph is velocity; for a curve, use the slope of the tangent line to get instantaneous velocity.
The slope of a velocity vs. time graph is acceleration, and the area under it is displacement.
Real-world planning combines map-scale measurements with distance, speed, and time relationships.

sections.title: Key Terms of One-Dimensional Kinematics
sections.body_markdown:
**Kinematics** is the study of motion without considering its causes. To describe motion, we need a shared vocabulary.

- **Reference frame:** a coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described. A description of motion *depends on* the reference frame, so you should always specify one.
- **Position:** the location of an object at any particular time.
- **Magnitude:** size or amount.
- **Scalar:** a quantity that has magnitude (and possibly sign) but no direction. Examples are distance and speed.
- **Vector:** a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Examples are displacement and velocity.
- **Instantaneous speed:** speed at a specific instant in time.
- **Instantaneous velocity:** velocity at a specific instant in time.
- **Acceleration:** the rate at which velocity changes.

**Reference frames in action**

Suppose you drive east past a friend standing at a bus stop. In your friend's frame, you are moving. In your frame, your friend is moving toward the west.

There is no single "correct" reference frame, because motion is relative. For example, a passenger on a moving train throws a ball straight up:

- A fellow passenger sees only vertical motion.
- An observer on the platform sees both vertical and horizontal motion.

sections.title: Distance vs. Displacement
sections.body_markdown:
- **Distance** is the length of the path actually traveled between an initial and a final position. It is a scalar.
- **Displacement** is the change in position of an object against a fixed axis. It is a vector, so it has magnitude and direction.

A car's **odometer** records distance, not displacement.

**Example 1: biker.** A biker rides 50 miles west, then 80 miles east.

- Distance = 50 + 80 = 130 miles.
- Displacement = 30 miles east.

**Example 2: round trips.** When an object returns to its starting point, its displacement is zero but its distance is not.

- A space shuttle that orbits Earth once travels a distance equal to the circumference of the orbit, but its displacement is zero.
- A bowling ball that rolls down the lane and is returned to the holder has zero displacement. Its distance is twice the lane length.

**Example 3: bouncing ball.** A ball is dropped from 1 m. It bounces to 0.8 m, then 0.5 m, then 0.2 m. Up is positive.

- Distance = 1 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 4 m.
- Displacement = –1 m, because the ball ends 1 m below where it started.

sections.title: Speed and Velocity
sections.body_markdown:
- **Speed** is the rate at which an object changes its location.
- **Average speed** = distance traveled ÷ time during which the motion occurs. It is a scalar.
- **Velocity** is the speed *and* direction of an object. It is a vector.
- **Average velocity** = displacement ÷ time over which the displacement occurs.

**How the quantities relate**

- The magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals the instantaneous speed.
- A speedometer shows speed but not direction. So it alone cannot give instantaneous velocity.
- If velocity is constant, average velocity and instantaneous velocity are the same.
- For a car moving at constant speed in one direction on a straight road, the magnitude of average velocity equals the average speed.

**Zero velocity with nonzero speed**

A swimmer completes 3 laps in 9 minutes, where one lap is across the pool and back. The swimmer's average velocity is zero because the total displacement is zero, even though the average speed is not zero.

sections.title: Solving Multi-Step Problems
sections.body_markdown:
Use this strategy:

1. Choose a positive direction.
2. Decide whether the question asks for a scalar (distance or speed) or a vector (displacement or velocity).
3. Convert units so they match.
4. Apply the definitions.

**Unit conversion.** A car moves at 86.4 km/h. How far does it travel in 3.3 s?

- Convert: 86.4 km/h = 24 m/s.
- Distance = 24 m/s × 3.3 s ≈ 79.2 m.

**Comparing average speeds.** Four cyclists travel these distances:

- Cyclist 1: 95 m in 27 s ≈ 3.5 m/s
- Cyclist 2: 87 m in 22 s ≈ 4.0 m/s
- Cyclist 3: 106 m in 26 s ≈ 4.1 m/s
- Cyclist 4: 108 m in 24 s = 4.5 m/s

Cyclist 4 has the greatest average speed.

**Limits on displacement.** A car averages 23 m/s for 82 s, so it travels about 1,886 m. Its displacement cannot be larger than its distance. A displacement of 2,000 m is therefore impossible.

**Same path, different speed.** A trip takes time t at average speed v. Returning along the same path at 3v takes t/3.

**Different paths, same endpoints.** A father walks straight to a bus stop 75 m away at 2.2 m/s. His daughter runs a varied path at 3.5 m/s, and they arrive at the same time.

- Time = 75 ÷ 2.2 ≈ 34 s.
- Daughter's distance ≈ 3.5 × 34 ≈ 119 m.
- In a straight line, she would have gone about 44 m beyond the stop.

**Round trip.** Alan walks 1.3 km east, 0.68 km east, 1.1 km north, and 0.42 km north, then returns home along the same path.

- Distance = 2 × 3.5 km = 7 km.
- Displacement = 0 km.

sections.title: Interpreting Position vs. Time Graphs
sections.body_markdown:
On a motion graph, the **independent variable** (usually time) goes on the horizontal axis. The **dependent variable** changes as the independent variable changes.

**Reading a position vs. time graph**

- The **slope** of a position vs. time graph is the velocity.
- For a straight-line graph, the slope is the average velocity.
- For a curved graph, find instantaneous velocity by drawing the **tangent** line at that point and taking its slope. A tangent is a line that touches the curve at exactly one point.

**Example: a train trip.** A train speeds up from rest for 15 min, cruises at 100 miles/hour for half an hour, then slows to a stop over 15 min. Its position graph has three parts:

- A concave-upward curve while speeding up.
- A straight line with slope 100 miles/hour while cruising.
- A concave-downward curve while slowing.

**Example: a hockey puck.** A puck travels 20 m out at constant speed, then is sent straight back. Its graph is a downward-opening V. The net displacement is 0 m, so the average velocity is 0 m/s, even though the distance is 40 m.

sections.title: Interpreting Velocity vs. Time Graphs
sections.body_markdown:
**Reading a velocity vs. time graph**

- The **slope** is the acceleration.
- The **area under the curve** is the displacement.
- Average velocity can be found by taking the weighted average of all the velocities.

**Example.** A car moving at 10 m/s doubles its velocity 10 s later. The area under its velocity graph gives the car's displacement during those 10 s.

**Estimating displacement from a curved graph**

- Divide the graph into sections.
- Find the area of each section.
- Add the areas together.

Using more divisions follows the curve more closely. In one review problem, seven divisions and two divisions gave different estimates of displacement (14,312.5 m vs. 15,500 m).

**Data needed for acceleration.** To estimate average acceleration from position measurements, you need at least three data points.

sections.title: Applying Kinematics to a Real-World Map Task
sections.body_markdown:
The chapter's performance task asks you to plan logistics for a concert on the National Mall in Washington, DC. You use a map scale to measure the distances you need.

**Part 1: Wire lengths**

Long-distance speakers can project sound up to 0.35 miles. They must be wired to a power supply in the concert area.

1. Trace the allowed path for the wire. Wire cannot go over buildings or memorials, and in one case it cannot cross water.
2. Measure the path on the map and convert it with the scale.
3. The speaker only needs to get within 0.35 miles of the target. Use this to find the *minimum* wire length.

**Part 2: Motorcade speed**

The motorcade travels a route along streets: west on E Street, then south on 23rd Street.

1. Measure each leg of the route and add them to get the total distance in miles.
2. Convert 5 minutes to hours: 5/60 h.
3. Minimum speed = distance ÷ time.

**Part 3: Helicopter time**

The helicopter flies directly from one landing zone to the other.

1. Measure the straight-line distance between the landing zones.
2. Time = distance ÷ 30 mph.
3. Convert the result to minutes.

**Key insight:** the motorcade's path length (a distance) is longer than the helicopter's straight-line path, which matches the size of the displacement.

visualization_candidates.concept: Reference frames: a ball thrown upward inside a moving train, seen by a passenger and by a platform observer
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Switching between the two viewpoints shows directly why one observer sees only vertical motion while the other sees vertical and horizontal motion.

visualization_candidates.concept: Linking an object's motion to its position vs. time graph and tangent slope
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Animating a moving object alongside a graph that is drawn in real time, with a moving tangent line, connects slope to instantaneous velocity.

visualization_candidates.concept: Distance vs. displacement for a bouncing ball or round trip
visualization_candidates.learning_reason: Tracking the accumulated path length alongside the net displacement arrow makes the difference between the scalar and the vector clear.

assessments.title: How Cells Are Studied: Chapter Quiz

options.text: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
Tissue → cell → organ → organism → organ system
Cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism

questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly shows how the parts of a multicellular organism are organized, from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation_correct: Cells of one kind interconnect and share functions to form tissues. Several tissues combine to form an organ. Several organs make up an organ system, and several systems working together form an organism.
questions.explanation_general: Start with the smallest unit of life, the cell, and ask what forms when several of each unit work together.

options.text: All body cells are identical and perform the same function.
Different cell types are specialized for specific purposes, yet all cells share fundamental characteristics.
Only immune cells are vital to the body's day-to-day maintenance.
Specialized cells share no common features with one another.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes how different cell types contribute to the human body?
questions.explanation_correct: The body contains many cell types, each specialized for a specific purpose. For example, red blood cells carry oxygen and bone cells support and protect the body. Despite this variety, all cells share certain fundamental characteristics.
questions.explanation_general: Think of the brick-wall analogy: the cells are the building blocks, but the body uses many kinds of them.

options.text: A transmission electron microscope, because it has the highest resolving power
A light microscope, because it can be used to view living organisms
A scanning electron microscope, because it shows surface details of moving cells
Any electron microscope, because the vacuum keeps cells alive

questions.question_text: A student wants to watch living, single-celled organisms moving in pond water. Which microscope is most appropriate, and why?
questions.explanation_correct: Light microscopes are advantageous for viewing living organisms. Preparing a specimen for electron microscopy kills it, and the electron beam requires a vacuum, so live cells cannot be viewed that way.
questions.explanation_general: Higher magnification is not always better. Consider what happens to a specimen when it is prepared for each type of microscope.

options.text: It has higher magnification and produces an inverted image.
It has lower magnification, gives a three-dimensional upright view, and can examine thick objects.
It uses a beam of electrons and requires a vacuum.
It can only view thin, translucent samples lit from below.

questions.question_text: How does a dissecting microscope differ from a typical light microscope used in a college lab?
questions.explanation_correct: Dissecting microscopes magnify about 20 to 80 times, which is lower than light microscopes. They give a three-dimensional view of thick objects. Their optics correct the image so it is not inverted, and light usually comes from above the sample.
questions.explanation_general: Dissecting microscopes are designed for larger objects, such as tissues and whole organisms. Think about what that requires in magnification and image orientation.

questions.question_text: Which term refers to a microscope's ability to let the eye distinguish two adjacent structures as separate?
questions.explanation_correct: Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two adjacent structures as separate. The higher the resolution, the closer the two objects can be and the better the clarity and detail of the image.
questions.explanation_general: Magnification only enlarges an object. Enlarging it does not necessarily make its details clearer.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to see the internal structures of a cell in fine detail. Which instrument should she use?
questions.explanation_correct: In a transmission electron microscope, the electron beam is transmitted through the cell and provides details of its internal structures.
questions.explanation_general: A scanning electron microscope moves its beam across the cell's surface and works by reflection, so it shows surface features rather than interior details.

questions.question_text: Which scientist coined the term "cell" after observing box-like structures in cork tissue?
questions.explanation_correct: In his 1665 publication Micrographia, Robert Hooke coined the term "cell" from the Latin cella, meaning "small room".
questions.explanation_general: Van Leeuwenhoek is known for observing "animalcules", bacteria and protozoa. Schleiden and Schwann proposed the unified cell theory.

rubric.description: States that in a scanning electron microscope the beam moves back and forth across the cell's surface and reveals surface details by reflection (a metal coating such as gold may also be mentioned).
States that in a transmission electron microscope the beam is transmitted through the cell and reveals internal structures.
Explains that specimen preparation kills the cells and/or that the electron beam requires a vacuum, so living cells cannot be viewed.

questions.model_answer: In a scanning electron microscope (SEM), a beam of electrons moves back and forth across the cell's surface, which is usually coated with a metal like gold. It shows surface details by reflection. In a transmission electron microscope (TEM), the beam passes through the cell and reveals its internal structures. Neither can be used to view living cells, because preparing the specimen kills it and the electron beam moves best in a vacuum.
questions.question_text: Compare scanning and transmission electron microscopes. For each one, explain how the electron beam interacts with the cell and what kind of information it provides. Then state one reason why neither can be used to view living cells.
questions.explanation_correct: SEM reflects electrons off the surface to show surface details. TEM transmits electrons through the cell to show internal structures. Both require specimen preparation that kills the cells, plus a vacuum.
questions.explanation_general: Focus on where the beam goes: across the surface or through the cell.

rubric.description: States that all living things are composed of one or more cells.
States that the cell is the basic unit of life.
States that all new cells arise from existing cells.
Names Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann.

questions.model_answer: The unified cell theory states that (1) all living things are composed of one or more cells, (2) the cell is the basic unit of life, and (3) all new cells arise from existing cells. It was proposed by botanist Matthias Schleiden and zoologist Theodor Schwann in the late 1830s.
questions.question_text: State the three principles of the unified cell theory and name the two scientists who proposed it.
questions.explanation_correct: Schleiden and Schwann proposed the theory in the late 1830s. It states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that new cells arise from existing cells.
questions.explanation_general: Remember that the theory was built on observations of tissues by both a botanist and a zoologist.

questions.question_text: Which of the following organisms is classified as a prokaryote?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotes are the predominantly single-celled organisms of the domains Bacteria and Archaea, so a bacterium is a prokaryote.
questions.explanation_general: Being single-celled does not by itself make an organism a prokaryote. Many protists are single-celled but are eukaryotes. Ask which domains prokaryotes belong to.

questions.question_text: Which group listed below consists entirely of eukaryotes?
questions.explanation_correct: Animal cells, plant cells, fungi, and protists are all eukaryotes.
questions.explanation_general: Archaea and Bacteria are both prokaryotic domains. Any option that includes either of them cannot be entirely eukaryotic.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four components shared by all cells?
questions.explanation_correct: All cells share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. A nucleus is found only in eukaryotic cells, because prokaryotes lack one.
questions.explanation_general: Think about what prokaryotes lack. A structure that is missing in prokaryotes cannot be shared by all cells.

questions.question_text: Which component found in all cells is responsible for synthesizing proteins?
questions.explanation_correct: Ribosomes are the particles that synthesize proteins.
questions.explanation_general: DNA carries genetic information, but it does not build proteins itself. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like region where cellular components are found.

options.text: In a central region called the nucleoid

questions.question_text: Where is the DNA of a prokaryotic cell located?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotic DNA is found in a darkened central region called the nucleoid. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus.
questions.explanation_general: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles, so their DNA cannot be enclosed by a membrane.

options.text: A cell wall made of peptidoglycan

questions.question_text: Which feature distinguishes bacteria from both Archaea and eukaryotes?
questions.explanation_correct: Unlike Archaea and eukaryotes, bacteria have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, which is made of sugars and amino acids.
questions.explanation_general: Ribosomes and a plasma membrane are found in all cells. A membrane-bound nucleus is a eukaryotic feature, not a bacterial one.

options.text: Prokaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm; eukaryotic cells are 10–100 µm
Prokaryotic cells are 10–100 µm; eukaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm

questions.question_text: How do the typical diameters of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells compare?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm in diameter, which is significantly smaller than eukaryotic cells at 10–100 µm.
questions.explanation_general: The size ranges do not overlap, and eukaryotes are the larger cells. Their large size is possible only because of structural adaptations that enhance cellular transport.

options.text: Volume increases much more quickly than surface area as a cell grows
Surface area increases much more quickly than volume as a cell grows
Surface area and volume increase at the same rate, so the membrane becomes too thick
Larger cells cannot contain enough ribosomes

questions.question_text: Why is cell size generally limited?
questions.explanation_correct: As a cell grows, its volume increases much more quickly than its surface area. The surface area available for transporting materials therefore becomes relatively smaller.
questions.explanation_general: A common mistake is to think surface area grows faster than volume, or that the two grow equally. The real problem is the declining ratio of surface area to volume.

rubric.description: States that as a cell grows, volume increases much more quickly than surface area.
Explains that the relative surface area for transporting materials declines, which makes it hard to acquire enough materials to support processes inside the cell.
Notes that small prokaryotes allow ions and organic molecules to spread quickly through the cell and wastes to move out quickly.

questions.model_answer: As a cell gets larger, its volume increases much faster than its surface area. The relative surface area across which materials must be transported therefore shrinks, and it becomes difficult for the cell to acquire enough materials to support its internal processes. Prokaryotes are small (0.1–5.0 µm), so ions and organic molecules that enter them spread quickly to other parts of the cell, and wastes can quickly move out.
questions.question_text: Explain how the relationship between surface area and volume limits cell size. Include why small prokaryotic cells benefit from their size.
questions.explanation_correct: Volume grows faster than surface area, so larger cells have relatively less membrane surface for exchanging materials. Small prokaryotes can quickly distribute incoming molecules and remove wastes.
questions.explanation_general: Connect the surface area to volume relationship with the cell's ability to move materials in and out.

rubric.description: Correctly names all four shared components: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes.
Describes the difference in DNA location and organization: prokaryotes have a nucleoid with no nucleus, while eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Describes a second valid difference, such as eukaryotes having membrane-bound organelles or the size difference (0.1–5.0 µm vs. 10–100 µm).

questions.model_answer: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, and their DNA sits in a central region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus. Eukaryotes also have membrane-bound organelles with specialized functions, which prokaryotes lack. Finally, prokaryotes are much smaller (0.1–5.0 µm) than eukaryotes (10–100 µm).
questions.question_text: Compare and contrast prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Identify the components they share and describe two structural differences.
questions.explanation_correct: Both cell types share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, while prokaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleoid and lack membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes are also much smaller.
questions.explanation_general: First list the shared components, then focus on nuclear organization, organelles, and size.

assessments.title: Chapter Quiz: Reference Frames, Distance, and Displacement

questions.question_text: You want to describe the position of a passenger walking down the aisle of a flying airplane. Which reference frame does the textbook say is used in this case?
questions.explanation_correct: The text states that to describe the position of a person in an airplane, we use the airplane, not Earth, as the reference frame. Reference frames do not have to be stationary relative to Earth.
questions.explanation_general: Earth is often used as a reference frame, but not always. Choose the background that is most convenient for describing the motion.

options.text: I see the train moving past me, and the rider sees me as stationary.
I see the train moving past me, and the rider sees me moving past the train.
I see the train as stationary, and the rider sees me moving past the train.
We both see each other as stationary.

questions.question_text: You stand on a platform watching a train pass by. According to Galileo's conclusions, how do your description of the motion and that of a person riding the train compare?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo concluded that descriptions of motion by two observers are symmetric or opposite. You see the train moving past you, and the rider sees you moving past the train.
questions.explanation_general: Neither observer is 'really' at rest. Each describes the other as moving relative to themselves.

questions.question_text: A parent drives you 5 km along a straight road to school, then drives back home. For the entire round trip, what are the distance traveled and the displacement?
questions.explanation_correct: Distance is the length of the path: 5 km + 5 km = 10 km. Displacement is the net change in position. The car ends where it started, so the displacement is 0.
questions.explanation_general: Distance adds up the whole path. Displacement compares only the final and initial positions, so opposite movements cancel.

options.text: The distance equals the track's perimeter, and the displacement is zero.
The distance and the displacement both equal the track's perimeter.
The distance is zero, and the displacement equals the track's perimeter.
The distance and the displacement are both zero.

questions.question_text: A race car completes exactly one lap around an oval track, finishing at the same line where it started. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation_correct: The distance is the length of the path, which is the perimeter of the track. The start and finish are at the same point, so the net change in position is zero.
questions.explanation_general: Don't confuse the length of the path with the net change in position. A closed loop returns the car to its starting position.

questions.question_text: Which of the following quantities is a vector?
questions.explanation_correct: A vector has both magnitude and direction, and the text gives displacement as an example. Distance and speed have magnitude but no direction, so they are scalars. Temperature in Celsius can have a sign but no direction, so it is also a scalar.
questions.explanation_general: A sign alone (such as a negative temperature) does not make a quantity a vector. Ask whether the quantity includes a direction.

questions.question_text: A student walks 12 m east and then 20 m west along a straight line. East is chosen as positive. What are the student's displacement and distance?
questions.explanation_correct: Displacement = +12 m + (−20 m) = −8 m, which is 8 m west. Distance = 12 m + 20 m = 32 m. Distance is always positive because direction does not matter for it.
questions.explanation_general: Direction affects displacement but not distance. A distance can never be negative.

questions.question_text: A height is given as 6,562 feet. Before using it in an SI calculation, you convert it to kilometers. What is the height in kilometers? (Assume 1 meter equals 3.281 feet.)
questions.explanation_correct: 6,562 ft ÷ 3.281 ft/m = 2,000 m, and 2,000 m = 2.0 km. The SI unit of length is the meter, so you convert to meters first.
questions.explanation_general: Since 1 m is longer than 1 ft, the number of meters must be smaller than the number of feet. Divide by 3.281 rather than multiplying.

options.text: Calculations were done in English units and not converted to SI units.
The wrong reference frame (the Sun instead of Mars) was chosen.
Distance was used instead of displacement.
The orbiter was launched with too little fuel.

questions.question_text: Why did the Mars Climate Orbiter fail?
questions.explanation_correct: The scientists made calculations in English units (feet, inches, pounds) and forgot to convert them to standard SI units. As a result, the orbiter flew into the Martian atmosphere and disintegrated.
questions.explanation_general: This case shows why all quantities must be in the same unit system, preferably SI, before you calculate.

rubric.description: Correctly finds the final position df = +25 m using signs (north +, south −).
Correctly applies Δd = df − d0 to get a displacement of +25 m (25 m north), including direction.
Correctly finds the distance as 55 m, with no sign or direction.

questions.model_answer: (a) df = 0 + 40 m − 15 m = +25 m. (b) Δd = df − d0 = 25 m − 0 = +25 m, which is 25 m north. (c) Distance = 40 m + 15 m = 55 m.
questions.question_text: A student starts at the origin (d0 = 0 m) and walks 40 m north, then turns around and walks 15 m south along the same straight line. North is positive. Find (a) the final position df, (b) the displacement, and (c) the distance traveled. Show how you used the chosen origin and positive direction.
questions.explanation_correct: Final position: df = 0 + 40 m − 15 m = +25 m. Displacement: Δd = df − d0 = 25 m − 0 m = +25 m, which is 25 m north. Distance: 40 m + 15 m = 55 m.
questions.explanation_general: Use Δd = df − d0, with northward motion taken as positive and southward motion as negative. Distance ignores direction.

rubric.description: States that motion is relative / depends on the observer's reference frame.
Explains that a description of motion is only meaningful once the reference frame (the background or coordinate system against which positions are measured) is specified.
Gives an appropriate example from the chapter showing different descriptions from different frames.

questions.model_answer: Motion is relative: you can only tell that an object moves, and in which direction, against a background that is either stationary or moving with a known speed and direction. Different observers can describe the same motion differently. A person on a train platform sees the train moving past, while a rider on the train sees the person on the platform moving past. A description of motion is therefore only meaningful if the reference frame is specified.
questions.question_text: Explain why a reference frame must be specified when describing motion. Support your answer with one example from the chapter, such as the train, the classroom, or Galileo's ship.
questions.explanation_correct: Motion is relative: the same motion is described differently from different reference frames. For example, riders on a fast train may not notice they are moving unless they look out the window. Meanwhile, someone on the platform sees the train moving past.
questions.explanation_general: Galileo concluded that a description of motion is only meaningful if a reference frame is specified.

options.text: A coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described
The single correct viewpoint, fixed to Earth, from which all motion must be described
A physical influence that changes the motion of an object
The length of the path an object travels

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly defines a reference frame?
questions.explanation_correct: A reference frame is a coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described. A description of motion depends on the reference frame used.
questions.explanation_general: A reference frame does not change how an object actually moves. It is the coordinate system you use to describe position and motion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following quantities is a scalar?
questions.explanation_correct: Average speed is distance traveled divided by time. It has magnitude but no direction, so it is a scalar.
questions.explanation_general: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity and displacement include direction, so they are vectors.

options.text: They are always identical, even when the direction changes.
The magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals instantaneous speed.
The magnitude of instantaneous velocity is always greater than instantaneous speed.
They can never be equal in magnitude.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the relationship between instantaneous velocity and instantaneous speed?
questions.explanation_correct: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a specific instant, and it includes direction. Its magnitude equals the instantaneous speed.
questions.explanation_general: Velocity adds direction to speed. The magnitude, or size, of velocity at an instant is the same as the speed at that instant.

questions.question_text: Billy drops a ball from a height of 1 m. It bounces to 0.8 m, then to 0.5 m, then to 0.2 m, and finally lands on the ground. Up is positive. What are the ball's total displacement and total distance traveled?
questions.explanation_correct: Displacement depends only on the start and end positions. The ball starts 1 m up and ends on the ground, so the displacement is −1 m. Distance adds every path segment: 1 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 4 m.
questions.explanation_general: Distance counts every up and down movement. Displacement compares only the initial and final positions and includes a sign for direction.

questions.question_text: You sit in a car moving at an average speed of 86.4 km/h. During the 3.3 s you glance out the window, how far does the car travel?
questions.explanation_correct: First convert the speed: 86.4 km/h = 24 m/s. Then distance = speed × time = 24 m/s × 3.3 s = 79.2 m.
questions.explanation_general: Convert units before multiplying. Multiplying km/h directly by seconds gives a result that makes no sense.

questions.question_text: Alan walks 1.3 km east to the library, then 0.68 km east to a music store. He then walks 1.1 km north to a friend's house and 0.42 km north to a grocery store. Finally, he returns home along the same path. What are his final displacement and total distance traveled?
questions.explanation_correct: The outbound trip is 1.3 + 0.68 + 1.1 + 0.42 = 3.5 km. Returning along the same path doubles this to 7 km of distance. He ends where he started, so his displacement is 0 km.
questions.explanation_general: Count both the outbound and return trips when finding distance. Displacement depends only on where he starts and ends.

options.text: Slope is acceleration; area is velocity
Slope is velocity; area is displacement
Slope is displacement; area is acceleration
Slope is distance; area is speed

questions.question_text: What is the slope of a straight-line position vs. time graph, and what does the area under a velocity vs. time graph represent?
questions.explanation_correct: The slope of a position vs. time graph is the velocity; for a straight line, it is the average velocity. The area under a velocity vs. time curve is the displacement.
questions.explanation_general: Do not mix up the two graphs. The slope of a velocity vs. time graph is acceleration, but the slope of a position vs. time graph is velocity.

options.text: Find the area under the curve up to that moment
Find the slope of the line connecting the first and last points of the graph
Find the slope of the tangent line at that point
Read the position value at that moment

questions.question_text: A position vs. time graph is curved. How do you find the instantaneous velocity at a particular moment?
questions.explanation_correct: For a curved position graph, draw the tangent line at that point. The slope of the tangent line is the instantaneous velocity.
questions.explanation_general: The slope between the endpoints gives only the average velocity. Instantaneous velocity requires the tangent line at the specific point.

questions.question_text: You are planning concert logistics. Using the map scale, you measure the motorcade's route from the White House (west on E Street, then south on 23rd Street) to the Lincoln Memorial as 1.0 mile. What minimum speed, in mph to the nearest tenth, does the motorcade need to make the trip in 5 minutes?
questions.explanation_correct: 5 minutes = 5/60 h ≈ 0.0833 h. Speed = distance ÷ time = 1.0 mi ÷ (5/60 h) = 12.0 mph.
questions.explanation_general: Convert minutes to hours before dividing to get miles per hour. Dividing miles by minutes gives miles per minute instead.

rubric.description: Finds the time: t = 75 m ÷ 2.2 m/s ≈ 34 s
Finds the daughter's distance: 3.5 m/s × 34 s ≈ 119 m
Finds the extra distance: 119 m − 75 m ≈ 44 m

questions.question_text: A father and his daughter go to a bus stop 75 m from their front door. The father walks in a straight line, while the daughter runs along a varied path. They arrive at the same time. The father's average speed is 2.2 m/s, and the daughter's is 3.5 m/s. (a) How long does the trip take? (b) What total distance did the daughter travel?
