(c) If she had kept the same average speed but traveled in a straight line, how far beyond the bus stop would she have gone?
questions.explanation_correct: Time = distance ÷ speed for the father. Since both arrive together, use that same time with the daughter's speed to get her distance.
questions.explanation_general: Use the father's straight-line trip to find the shared time. Then apply the daughter's average speed to that time.

rubric.description: Uses time = distance ÷ speed: 0.9 mi ÷ 30 mph = 0.03 h
Converts to minutes: 0.03 h × 60 = 1.8 min
Rounds correctly to 2 minutes

questions.model_answer: t = 0.9 mi ÷ 30 mph = 0.03 h = 1.8 min ≈ 2 minutes.
questions.question_text: For the concert planning task, the president could fly on Marine 1 from directly above the White House landing zone to directly above the Lincoln Memorial landing zone. Suppose you use the map scale to measure this straight-line distance as 0.9 miles. Ignoring liftoff and landing, how long would the trip take at 30 mph? Report your answer in minutes to the nearest minute and show your work.
questions.explanation_correct: Rearrange the speed equation to time = distance ÷ speed. Then convert hours to minutes.
questions.explanation_general: Divide distance by speed to get time in hours, then multiply by 60 to get minutes.

snapshot.title: How Cells Are Studied: Chapter Quiz

options.text: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
Tissue → cell → organ → organism → organ system
Cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism

questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly shows how the parts of a multicellular organism are organized, from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation_correct: Cells of one kind interconnect and share functions to form tissues. Several tissues combine to form an organ. Several organs make up an organ system, and several systems working together form an organism.
questions.explanation_general: Start with the smallest unit of life, the cell, and ask what forms when several of each unit work together.

options.text: All body cells are identical and perform the same function.
Different cell types are specialized for specific purposes, yet all cells share fundamental characteristics.
Only immune cells are vital to the body's day-to-day maintenance.
Specialized cells share no common features with one another.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes how different cell types contribute to the human body?
questions.explanation_correct: The body contains many cell types, each specialized for a specific purpose. For example, red blood cells carry oxygen and bone cells support and protect the body. Despite this variety, all cells share certain fundamental characteristics.
questions.explanation_general: Think of the brick-wall analogy: the cells are the building blocks, but the body uses many kinds of them.

options.text: A transmission electron microscope, because it has the highest resolving power
A light microscope, because it can be used to view living organisms
A scanning electron microscope, because it shows surface details of moving cells
Any electron microscope, because the vacuum keeps cells alive

questions.question_text: A student wants to watch living, single-celled organisms moving in pond water. Which microscope is most appropriate, and why?
questions.explanation_correct: Light microscopes are advantageous for viewing living organisms. Preparing a specimen for electron microscopy kills it, and the electron beam requires a vacuum, so live cells cannot be viewed that way.
questions.explanation_general: Higher magnification is not always better. Consider what happens to a specimen when it is prepared for each type of microscope.

options.text: It has higher magnification and produces an inverted image.
It has lower magnification, gives a three-dimensional upright view, and can examine thick objects.
It uses a beam of electrons and requires a vacuum.
It can only view thin, translucent samples lit from below.

questions.question_text: How does a dissecting microscope differ from a typical light microscope used in a college lab?
questions.explanation_correct: Dissecting microscopes magnify about 20 to 80 times, which is lower than light microscopes. They give a three-dimensional view of thick objects. Their optics correct the image so it is not inverted, and light usually comes from above the sample.
questions.explanation_general: Dissecting microscopes are designed for larger objects, such as tissues and whole organisms. Think about what that requires in magnification and image orientation.

questions.question_text: Which term refers to a microscope's ability to let the eye distinguish two adjacent structures as separate?
questions.explanation_correct: Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two adjacent structures as separate. The higher the resolution, the closer the two objects can be and the better the clarity and detail of the image.
questions.explanation_general: Magnification only enlarges an object. Enlarging it does not necessarily make its details clearer.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to see the internal structures of a cell in fine detail. Which instrument should she use?
questions.explanation_correct: In a transmission electron microscope, the electron beam is transmitted through the cell and provides details of its internal structures.
questions.explanation_general: A scanning electron microscope moves its beam across the cell's surface and works by reflection, so it shows surface features rather than interior details.

questions.question_text: Which scientist coined the term "cell" after observing box-like structures in cork tissue?
questions.explanation_correct: In his 1665 publication Micrographia, Robert Hooke coined the term "cell" from the Latin cella, meaning "small room".
questions.explanation_general: Van Leeuwenhoek is known for observing "animalcules", bacteria and protozoa. Schleiden and Schwann proposed the unified cell theory.

rubric.description: States that in a scanning electron microscope the beam moves back and forth across the cell's surface and reveals surface details by reflection (a metal coating such as gold may also be mentioned).
States that in a transmission electron microscope the beam is transmitted through the cell and reveals internal structures.
Explains that specimen preparation kills the cells and/or that the electron beam requires a vacuum, so living cells cannot be viewed.

questions.model_answer: In a scanning electron microscope (SEM), a beam of electrons moves back and forth across the cell's surface, which is usually coated with a metal like gold. It shows surface details by reflection. In a transmission electron microscope (TEM), the beam passes through the cell and reveals its internal structures. Neither can be used to view living cells, because preparing the specimen kills it and the electron beam moves best in a vacuum.
questions.question_text: Compare scanning and transmission electron microscopes. For each one, explain how the electron beam interacts with the cell and what kind of information it provides. Then state one reason why neither can be used to view living cells.
questions.explanation_correct: SEM reflects electrons off the surface to show surface details. TEM transmits electrons through the cell to show internal structures. Both require specimen preparation that kills the cells, plus a vacuum.
questions.explanation_general: Focus on where the beam goes: across the surface or through the cell.

rubric.description: States that all living things are composed of one or more cells.
States that the cell is the basic unit of life.
States that all new cells arise from existing cells.
Names Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann.

questions.model_answer: The unified cell theory states that (1) all living things are composed of one or more cells, (2) the cell is the basic unit of life, and (3) all new cells arise from existing cells. It was proposed by botanist Matthias Schleiden and zoologist Theodor Schwann in the late 1830s.
questions.question_text: State the three principles of the unified cell theory and name the two scientists who proposed it.
questions.explanation_correct: Schleiden and Schwann proposed the theory in the late 1830s. It states that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that new cells arise from existing cells.
questions.explanation_general: Remember that the theory was built on observations of tissues by both a botanist and a zoologist.

questions.question_text: Which of the following organisms is classified as a prokaryote?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotes are the predominantly single-celled organisms of the domains Bacteria and Archaea, so a bacterium is a prokaryote.
questions.explanation_general: Being single-celled does not by itself make an organism a prokaryote. Many protists are single-celled but are eukaryotes. Ask which domains prokaryotes belong to.

questions.question_text: Which group listed below consists entirely of eukaryotes?
questions.explanation_correct: Animal cells, plant cells, fungi, and protists are all eukaryotes.
questions.explanation_general: Archaea and Bacteria are both prokaryotic domains. Any option that includes either of them cannot be entirely eukaryotic.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four components shared by all cells?
questions.explanation_correct: All cells share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. A nucleus is found only in eukaryotic cells, because prokaryotes lack one.
questions.explanation_general: Think about what prokaryotes lack. A structure that is missing in prokaryotes cannot be shared by all cells.

questions.question_text: Which component found in all cells is responsible for synthesizing proteins?
questions.explanation_correct: Ribosomes are the particles that synthesize proteins.
questions.explanation_general: DNA carries genetic information, but it does not build proteins itself. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like region where cellular components are found.

options.text: In a central region called the nucleoid

questions.question_text: Where is the DNA of a prokaryotic cell located?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotic DNA is found in a darkened central region called the nucleoid. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus.
questions.explanation_general: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles, so their DNA cannot be enclosed by a membrane.

options.text: A cell wall made of peptidoglycan

questions.question_text: Which feature distinguishes bacteria from both Archaea and eukaryotes?
questions.explanation_correct: Unlike Archaea and eukaryotes, bacteria have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, which is made of sugars and amino acids.
questions.explanation_general: Ribosomes and a plasma membrane are found in all cells. A membrane-bound nucleus is a eukaryotic feature, not a bacterial one.

options.text: Prokaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm; eukaryotic cells are 10–100 µm
Prokaryotic cells are 10–100 µm; eukaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm

questions.question_text: How do the typical diameters of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells compare?
questions.explanation_correct: Prokaryotic cells are 0.1–5.0 µm in diameter, which is significantly smaller than eukaryotic cells at 10–100 µm.
questions.explanation_general: The size ranges do not overlap, and eukaryotes are the larger cells. Their large size is possible only because of structural adaptations that enhance cellular transport.

options.text: Volume increases much more quickly than surface area as a cell grows
Surface area increases much more quickly than volume as a cell grows
Surface area and volume increase at the same rate, so the membrane becomes too thick
Larger cells cannot contain enough ribosomes

questions.question_text: Why is cell size generally limited?
questions.explanation_correct: As a cell grows, its volume increases much more quickly than its surface area. The surface area available for transporting materials therefore becomes relatively smaller.
questions.explanation_general: A common mistake is to think surface area grows faster than volume, or that the two grow equally. The real problem is the declining ratio of surface area to volume.

rubric.description: States that as a cell grows, volume increases much more quickly than surface area.
Explains that the relative surface area for transporting materials declines, which makes it hard to acquire enough materials to support processes inside the cell.
Notes that small prokaryotes allow ions and organic molecules to spread quickly through the cell and wastes to move out quickly.

questions.model_answer: As a cell gets larger, its volume increases much faster than its surface area. The relative surface area across which materials must be transported therefore shrinks, and it becomes difficult for the cell to acquire enough materials to support its internal processes. Prokaryotes are small (0.1–5.0 µm), so ions and organic molecules that enter them spread quickly to other parts of the cell, and wastes can quickly move out.
questions.question_text: Explain how the relationship between surface area and volume limits cell size. Include why small prokaryotic cells benefit from their size.
questions.explanation_correct: Volume grows faster than surface area, so larger cells have relatively less membrane surface for exchanging materials. Small prokaryotes can quickly distribute incoming molecules and remove wastes.
questions.explanation_general: Connect the surface area to volume relationship with the cell's ability to move materials in and out.

rubric.description: Correctly names all four shared components: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes.
Describes the difference in DNA location and organization: prokaryotes have a nucleoid with no nucleus, while eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Describes a second valid difference, such as eukaryotes having membrane-bound organelles or the size difference (0.1–5.0 µm vs. 10–100 µm).

questions.model_answer: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, and their DNA sits in a central region called the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus. Eukaryotes also have membrane-bound organelles with specialized functions, which prokaryotes lack. Finally, prokaryotes are much smaller (0.1–5.0 µm) than eukaryotes (10–100 µm).
questions.question_text: Compare and contrast prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Identify the components they share and describe two structural differences.
questions.explanation_correct: Both cell types share a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, while prokaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleoid and lack membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes are also much smaller.
questions.explanation_general: First list the shared components, then focus on nuclear organization, organelles, and size.

snapshot.title: Chapter Quiz: Reference Frames, Distance, and Displacement

questions.question_text: You want to describe the position of a passenger walking down the aisle of a flying airplane. Which reference frame does the textbook say is used in this case?
questions.explanation_correct: The text states that to describe the position of a person in an airplane, we use the airplane, not Earth, as the reference frame. Reference frames do not have to be stationary relative to Earth.
questions.explanation_general: Earth is often used as a reference frame, but not always. Choose the background that is most convenient for describing the motion.

options.text: I see the train moving past me, and the rider sees me as stationary.
I see the train moving past me, and the rider sees me moving past the train.
I see the train as stationary, and the rider sees me moving past the train.
We both see each other as stationary.

questions.question_text: You stand on a platform watching a train pass by. According to Galileo's conclusions, how do your description of the motion and that of a person riding the train compare?
questions.explanation_correct: Galileo concluded that descriptions of motion by two observers are symmetric or opposite. You see the train moving past you, and the rider sees you moving past the train.
questions.explanation_general: Neither observer is 'really' at rest. Each describes the other as moving relative to themselves.

questions.question_text: A parent drives you 5 km along a straight road to school, then drives back home. For the entire round trip, what are the distance traveled and the displacement?
questions.explanation_correct: Distance is the length of the path: 5 km + 5 km = 10 km. Displacement is the net change in position. The car ends where it started, so the displacement is 0.
questions.explanation_general: Distance adds up the whole path. Displacement compares only the final and initial positions, so opposite movements cancel.

options.text: The distance equals the track's perimeter, and the displacement is zero.
The distance and the displacement both equal the track's perimeter.
The distance is zero, and the displacement equals the track's perimeter.
The distance and the displacement are both zero.

questions.question_text: A race car completes exactly one lap around an oval track, finishing at the same line where it started. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation_correct: The distance is the length of the path, which is the perimeter of the track. The start and finish are at the same point, so the net change in position is zero.
questions.explanation_general: Don't confuse the length of the path with the net change in position. A closed loop returns the car to its starting position.

questions.question_text: Which of the following quantities is a vector?
questions.explanation_correct: A vector has both magnitude and direction, and the text gives displacement as an example. Distance and speed have magnitude but no direction, so they are scalars. Temperature in Celsius can have a sign but no direction, so it is also a scalar.
questions.explanation_general: A sign alone (such as a negative temperature) does not make a quantity a vector. Ask whether the quantity includes a direction.

questions.question_text: A student walks 12 m east and then 20 m west along a straight line. East is chosen as positive. What are the student's displacement and distance?
questions.explanation_correct: Displacement = +12 m + (−20 m) = −8 m, which is 8 m west. Distance = 12 m + 20 m = 32 m. Distance is always positive because direction does not matter for it.
questions.explanation_general: Direction affects displacement but not distance. A distance can never be negative.

questions.question_text: A height is given as 6,562 feet. Before using it in an SI calculation, you convert it to kilometers. What is the height in kilometers? (Assume 1 meter equals 3.281 feet.)
questions.explanation_correct: 6,562 ft ÷ 3.281 ft/m = 2,000 m, and 2,000 m = 2.0 km. The SI unit of length is the meter, so you convert to meters first.
questions.explanation_general: Since 1 m is longer than 1 ft, the number of meters must be smaller than the number of feet. Divide by 3.281 rather than multiplying.

options.text: Calculations were done in English units and not converted to SI units.
The wrong reference frame (the Sun instead of Mars) was chosen.
Distance was used instead of displacement.
The orbiter was launched with too little fuel.

questions.question_text: Why did the Mars Climate Orbiter fail?
questions.explanation_correct: The scientists made calculations in English units (feet, inches, pounds) and forgot to convert them to standard SI units. As a result, the orbiter flew into the Martian atmosphere and disintegrated.
questions.explanation_general: This case shows why all quantities must be in the same unit system, preferably SI, before you calculate.

rubric.description: Correctly finds the final position df = +25 m using signs (north +, south −).
Correctly applies Δd = df − d0 to get a displacement of +25 m (25 m north), including direction.
Correctly finds the distance as 55 m, with no sign or direction.

questions.model_answer: (a) df = 0 + 40 m − 15 m = +25 m. (b) Δd = df − d0 = 25 m − 0 = +25 m, which is 25 m north. (c) Distance = 40 m + 15 m = 55 m.
questions.question_text: A student starts at the origin (d0 = 0 m) and walks 40 m north, then turns around and walks 15 m south along the same straight line. North is positive. Find (a) the final position df, (b) the displacement, and (c) the distance traveled. Show how you used the chosen origin and positive direction.
questions.explanation_correct: Final position: df = 0 + 40 m − 15 m = +25 m. Displacement: Δd = df − d0 = 25 m − 0 m = +25 m, which is 25 m north. Distance: 40 m + 15 m = 55 m.
questions.explanation_general: Use Δd = df − d0, with northward motion taken as positive and southward motion as negative. Distance ignores direction.

rubric.description: States that motion is relative / depends on the observer's reference frame.
Explains that a description of motion is only meaningful once the reference frame (the background or coordinate system against which positions are measured) is specified.
Gives an appropriate example from the chapter showing different descriptions from different frames.

questions.model_answer: Motion is relative: you can only tell that an object moves, and in which direction, against a background that is either stationary or moving with a known speed and direction. Different observers can describe the same motion differently. A person on a train platform sees the train moving past, while a rider on the train sees the person on the platform moving past. A description of motion is therefore only meaningful if the reference frame is specified.
questions.question_text: Explain why a reference frame must be specified when describing motion. Support your answer with one example from the chapter, such as the train, the classroom, or Galileo's ship.
questions.explanation_correct: Motion is relative: the same motion is described differently from different reference frames. For example, riders on a fast train may not notice they are moving unless they look out the window. Meanwhile, someone on the platform sees the train moving past.
questions.explanation_general: Galileo concluded that a description of motion is only meaningful if a reference frame is specified.

options.text: A coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described
The single correct viewpoint, fixed to Earth, from which all motion must be described
A physical influence that changes the motion of an object
The length of the path an object travels

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly defines a reference frame?
questions.explanation_correct: A reference frame is a coordinate system from which the positions of objects are described. A description of motion depends on the reference frame used.
questions.explanation_general: A reference frame does not change how an object actually moves. It is the coordinate system you use to describe position and motion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following quantities is a scalar?
questions.explanation_correct: Average speed is distance traveled divided by time. It has magnitude but no direction, so it is a scalar.
questions.explanation_general: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity and displacement include direction, so they are vectors.

options.text: They are always identical, even when the direction changes.
The magnitude of instantaneous velocity equals instantaneous speed.
The magnitude of instantaneous velocity is always greater than instantaneous speed.
They can never be equal in magnitude.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes the relationship between instantaneous velocity and instantaneous speed?
questions.explanation_correct: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a specific instant, and it includes direction. Its magnitude equals the instantaneous speed.
questions.explanation_general: Velocity adds direction to speed. The magnitude, or size, of velocity at an instant is the same as the speed at that instant.

questions.question_text: Billy drops a ball from a height of 1 m. It bounces to 0.8 m, then to 0.5 m, then to 0.2 m, and finally lands on the ground. Up is positive. What are the ball's total displacement and total distance traveled?
questions.explanation_correct: Displacement depends only on the start and end positions. The ball starts 1 m up and ends on the ground, so the displacement is −1 m. Distance adds every path segment: 1 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 4 m.
questions.explanation_general: Distance counts every up and down movement. Displacement compares only the initial and final positions and includes a sign for direction.

questions.question_text: You sit in a car moving at an average speed of 86.4 km/h. During the 3.3 s you glance out the window, how far does the car travel?
questions.explanation_correct: First convert the speed: 86.4 km/h = 24 m/s. Then distance = speed × time = 24 m/s × 3.3 s = 79.2 m.
questions.explanation_general: Convert units before multiplying. Multiplying km/h directly by seconds gives a result that makes no sense.

questions.question_text: Alan walks 1.3 km east to the library, then 0.68 km east to a music store. He then walks 1.1 km north to a friend's house and 0.42 km north to a grocery store. Finally, he returns home along the same path. What are his final displacement and total distance traveled?
questions.explanation_correct: The outbound trip is 1.3 + 0.68 + 1.1 + 0.42 = 3.5 km. Returning along the same path doubles this to 7 km of distance. He ends where he started, so his displacement is 0 km.
questions.explanation_general: Count both the outbound and return trips when finding distance. Displacement depends only on where he starts and ends.

options.text: Slope is acceleration; area is velocity
Slope is velocity; area is displacement
Slope is displacement; area is acceleration
Slope is distance; area is speed

questions.question_text: What is the slope of a straight-line position vs. time graph, and what does the area under a velocity vs. time graph represent?
questions.explanation_correct: The slope of a position vs. time graph is the velocity; for a straight line, it is the average velocity. The area under a velocity vs. time curve is the displacement.
questions.explanation_general: Do not mix up the two graphs. The slope of a velocity vs. time graph is acceleration, but the slope of a position vs. time graph is velocity.

options.text: Find the area under the curve up to that moment
Find the slope of the line connecting the first and last points of the graph
Find the slope of the tangent line at that point
Read the position value at that moment

questions.question_text: A position vs. time graph is curved. How do you find the instantaneous velocity at a particular moment?
questions.explanation_correct: For a curved position graph, draw the tangent line at that point. The slope of the tangent line is the instantaneous velocity.
questions.explanation_general: The slope between the endpoints gives only the average velocity. Instantaneous velocity requires the tangent line at the specific point.

questions.question_text: You are planning concert logistics. Using the map scale, you measure the motorcade's route from the White House (west on E Street, then south on 23rd Street) to the Lincoln Memorial as 1.0 mile. What minimum speed, in mph to the nearest tenth, does the motorcade need to make the trip in 5 minutes?
questions.explanation_correct: 5 minutes = 5/60 h ≈ 0.0833 h. Speed = distance ÷ time = 1.0 mi ÷ (5/60 h) = 12.0 mph.
questions.explanation_general: Convert minutes to hours before dividing to get miles per hour. Dividing miles by minutes gives miles per minute instead.

rubric.description: Finds the time: t = 75 m ÷ 2.2 m/s ≈ 34 s
Finds the daughter's distance: 3.5 m/s × 34 s ≈ 119 m
Finds the extra distance: 119 m − 75 m ≈ 44 m

questions.question_text: A father and his daughter go to a bus stop 75 m from their front door. The father walks in a straight line, while the daughter runs along a varied path. They arrive at the same time. The father's average speed is 2.2 m/s, and the daughter's is 3.5 m/s. (a) How long does the trip take? (b) What total distance did the daughter travel? (c) If she had kept the same average speed but traveled in a straight line, how far beyond the bus stop would she have gone?
questions.explanation_correct: Time = distance ÷ speed for the father. Since both arrive together, use that same time with the daughter's speed to get her distance.
questions.explanation_general: Use the father's straight-line trip to find the shared time. Then apply the daughter's average speed to that time.

rubric.description: Uses time = distance ÷ speed: 0.9 mi ÷ 30 mph = 0.03 h
Converts to minutes: 0.03 h × 60 = 1.8 min
Rounds correctly to 2 minutes

questions.model_answer: t = 0.9 mi ÷ 30 mph = 0.03 h = 1.8 min ≈ 2 minutes.
questions.question_text: For the concert planning task, the president could fly on Marine 1 from directly above the White House landing zone to directly above the Lincoln Memorial landing zone. Suppose you use the map scale to measure this straight-line distance as 0.9 miles. Ignoring liftoff and landing, how long would the trip take at 30 mph? Report your answer in minutes to the nearest minute and show your work.
questions.explanation_correct: Rearrange the speed equation to time = distance ÷ speed. Then convert hours to minutes.
questions.explanation_general: Divide distance by speed to get time in hours, then multiply by 60 to get minutes.

three_d_scenes.title: How the Parts of a Light Microscope Work Together

scene_spec.title: How the Parts of a Light Microscope Work Together

explanations.exp_arm: The upright support that joins the base to the body tube and holds the stage. You also use it to carry the microscope.
explanations.exp_base: The heavy, flat foot that keeps the microscope steady. It holds the built-in light source.
explanations.exp_stage: The flat platform where the slide sits. A hole in its centre, called the aperture, lets light from below pass through the specimen.
explanations.exp_specimen: The thin, see-through sample being studied. Light shines through it, so its details can be magnified.
explanations.exp_body_tube: The upright tube that keeps the objective and the eyepiece the right distance apart. It is cut open here to show the light path inside.
explanations.exp_light_beam: The glowing beam shows the path light takes. It goes from the light source up through the slide and specimen, then through the objective lens and the body tube, and finally out through the eyepiece.
explanations.exp_glass_slide: A thin, clear piece of glass that holds the specimen. Light passes through it easily.
explanations.exp_stage_clips: Two metal clips that hold the glass slide in place on the stage.
explanations.exp_light_source: A lamp in the base that shines light straight up. The light passes through the hole in the stage and through the specimen.
explanations.exp_eyepiece_lens: The lens at the top that magnifies the image from the objective again. Total magnification is the objective's magnification multiplied by the eyepiece's.
explanations.exp_objective_lens: The lens closest to the specimen. It makes the first magnified image, which travels up the body tube.
explanations.exp_eyepiece_housing: The short barrel at the top of the body tube that holds the eyepiece lens. You look into it with your eye.
explanations.exp_objective_housing: The metal barrel that holds the objective lens just above the slide. It is shown cut open so you can see the lens inside.

scene_spec.title: Motion in One Dimension: Cart, Motion Diagram and Graphs

explanations.exp_tick_marks: Evenly spaced marks every 0.2 units along the front edge of the track. They let you read positions and compare the distances between snapshots.
explanations.exp_ground_plate: A plain light-grey base that holds the whole diorama. It is only there for support and does not stand for any physics quantity.
explanations.exp_origin_marker: The reference point labelled 0. Positions are measured from here: positive to the right, negative to the left.
explanations.exp_free_fall_ball: A ball released from a vertical post, with faint copies lower down taken at equal time intervals. The gaps grow as it falls, showing that vertical free fall is also one-dimensional accelerated motion.
explanations.exp_acceleration_arrow: A red arrow pointing +x, the same direction as the velocity, so the cart speeds up. Its length is the same throughout the motion because the acceleration is constant.
explanations.exp_area_under_vt_line: The green trapezoid between the v–t line and the time axis. Its area equals the cart's displacement, which matches the green arrow on the track.
explanations.exp_displacement_arrow: A green arrow from the initial position (-0.8) to the final position (0.4). Displacement = x_final - x_initial = +1.2. It depends only on where the motion starts and ends.
explanations.exp_tangent_slope_line: An orange line touching the x–t curve at its last point. Its slope is the cart's instantaneous velocity at that moment.
explanations.exp_velocity_time_line: A straight line that starts above zero (the cart is already moving) and rises steadily. Its constant slope is the acceleration.
explanations.exp_cart_final_position: The solid yellow cart at x = 0.4, its position at the end of the fourth time interval. The displacement arrow ends here.
explanations.exp_position_time_curve: An upward-curving parabola for constant acceleration. The five dots at equal time steps match the five cart positions. The curve gets steeper because the velocity keeps increasing.
explanations.exp_position_time_graph: A panel with a time axis (t) and a position axis (x). It shows how the cart's position changes over time.
explanations.exp_track_position_axis: A straight track that works as a number line along the x-axis, from x = -1 to x = +1. The cart's position at any moment is a single number on this line, so the motion is one-dimensional.
explanations.exp_velocity_time_graph: A panel with a time axis (t) and a velocity axis (v). It shows how the cart's velocity changes over time.
explanations.exp_velocity_arrow_final: A longer blue arrow showing the cart's higher velocity at the end. It is longer than the initial arrow because the cart sped up.
explanations.exp_cart_initial_position: A see-through cart at x = -0.8 showing where the motion starts (t = 0). The displacement arrow begins here.
explanations.exp_motion_diagram_ghosts: Faint copies of the cart at x = -0.65, -0.4 and -0.05, taken at equal time intervals. Including the initial and final carts, the gaps grow by 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 and 0.45. Gaps that grow by the same amount each interval mean constant acceleration.
explanations.exp_velocity_arrow_initial: A short blue arrow showing that the cart is already moving slowly in the +x direction at the start. A shorter arrow means a lower speed.
explanations.exp_gravity_acceleration_arrow: A red arrow pointing straight down, labelled g. In free fall the acceleration is constant and always points downward, about 9.8 m/s².
explanations.exp_positive_direction_indicator: The white arrow and '+x' plate set +x as the positive direction. Any vector pointing this way has a positive sign.

three_d_assets.name: The Human Brain: Major Regions and Structures
three_d_assets.description:
AI-generated from prompt: 1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
An interactive model for middle to high school biology students. They should identify the main external regions of the brain (the four cerebral lobes, cerebellum, brainstem) and key internal structures (corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, pituitary gland, ventricles). They should also understand where each part sits relative to the others. Each region is a separate, clickable mesh with a distinct colour.

2. OVERALL FORM
Build a stylised adult human brain, about 2 units long front-to-back (Y axis), centred at the origin, with Z up. The front (frontal pole) points toward -Y. The left hemisphere is on -X.
- Right hemisphere: complete, with the external lobes.
- Left hemisphere: shown as a midsagittal cutaway. The left hemisphere is removed so the flat medial (inner) face of the right hemisphere faces -X and the internal midline structures are exposed. Put the internal midline structures on this cut face.
The best view is from the front-left at an elevation of about 20 degrees, so students see the lateral lobes and the cut medial face. Overall proportions: length 2.0, height about 1.5, width of the single hemisphere about 0.75. Give the cortex a gently bumpy surface. Suggest gyri and sulci with displacement or shallow grooves, but keep the lobes as clean separate shapes.

3. PARTS
- frontal_lobe - The front of the cerebrum, extending back to the central sulcus at about the midpoint of the top. It is the largest lobe, about 1/3 of the hemisphere. Colour: blue.
- parietal_lobe - Sits behind the frontal lobe and above the temporal lobe, running from the central sulcus to the parieto-occipital sulcus. Colour: yellow.
- temporal_lobe - The lower side lobe, below the lateral (Sylvian) fissure. Shaped like a thumb pointing forward. Colour: green.
- occipital_lobe - The rear pole of the cerebrum, the smallest lobe. Colour: orange.
- cerebellum - A rounded, finely ridged structure with horizontal folia grooves. It sits under the occipital lobe at the back, behind the brainstem. About 1/4 of the brain's length. Colour: purple.
- brainstem - A tapered column below the centre of the brain, angled slightly forward. Divide it into three stacked segments:
  - midbrain (top, short, light pink)
  - pons (middle, bulging forward, salmon)
  - medulla_oblongata (bottom, narrowing, rose)
- spinal_cord_stub - A short cylinder continuing below the medulla, cut off. Colour: pale grey.
- corpus_callosum - On the cut medial face: a thick C-shaped (arched) band of white fibres above the thalamus. It spans about the middle half of the brain's length. Colour: white.
- lateral_ventricle - A thin, curved, fluid-filled cavity just below the corpus callosum, visible on the cut face. Colour: light cyan, semi-transparent.
- thalamus - An egg-shaped mass in the centre, below the corpus callosum and on top of the brainstem. Colour: teal.
- hypothalamus - A small region just below and in front of the thalamus. Colour: magenta.
- pituitary_gland - A pea-sized ball hanging on a thin stalk below the hypothalamus. Colour: red.
- hippocampus - A curved, seahorse-like tube deep in the medial temporal lobe, below and behind the thalamus. Show it as slightly protruding on the cut face. Colour: gold.
- amygdala - A small almond shape just in front of the hippocampus tip. Colour: dark red.
- olfactory_bulb - A thin rod with a bulb end under the frontal lobe, pointing forward. Colour: light green.
- central_sulcus - A visible groove separating the frontal and parietal lobes. Model it as a thin dark curved strip mesh. Colour: dark grey.
- lateral_fissure - A deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. Model it as a dark strip. Colour: dark grey.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
Use the midsagittal cut described above. No transparent shell is needed. The cut face of the cortex should be a slightly darker tone of each lobe's colour, to suggest grey matter, with lighter interior. The deep structures sit flush with or slightly raised from the cut plane:
- thalamus
- hypothalamus
- corpus callosum
- ventricle
- hippocampus
- amygdala

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- Four lobes per hemisphere.
- The cerebellum is posterior and inferior, never above the cerebrum.
- The brainstem connects the cerebrum (via the midbrain at the thalamus) to the spinal cord.
- The pons bulges anteriorly.
- The corpus callosum is above the thalamus and ventricle.
- The pituitary is below the hypothalamus, connected by a stalk.
- The hippocampus lies within the temporal lobe, medial side.
- The olfactory bulb is on the underside of the frontal lobe.
- The cerebrum is by far the largest part, about 80-85% of the volume.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
Omit the following:
- blood vessels
- meninges
- cranial nerves (other than the olfactory bulb)
- basal ganglia
- detailed individual gyri names
- skull
Use smooth stylised shapes and flat, clearly distinct colours, with no photorealistic textures. Name each mesh object exact…

three_d_assets.name: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cells
three_d_assets.description:
AI-generated from prompt: 1. Purpose and audience: Middle/high school biology students compare a prokaryotic cell (bacterium) with a eukaryotic cell (generalised animal cell) side by side. They should see that prokaryotes are much smaller and lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (their DNA sits free in a nucleoid region), while eukaryotes have a nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles. Both share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

2. Overall form: Two cells sit on a flat, light-grey oval base plate (base_plate is not a clickable teaching part; name it 'display_base'). Z is up. The whole scene is about 2 units across, centred at the origin. The eukaryotic cell is on the right (+X), a rounded blob about 1.1 units in diameter, centred near x=+0.4. The prokaryotic cell is on the left (-X), a capsule (rod) about 0.45 units long and 0.18 wide, centred near x=-0.7, lying horizontally. The size difference is deliberate but still exaggerated for visibility (real eukaryotes are ~10-100x larger); keep the prokaryote clearly much smaller. Best view: three-quarter from front-above (camera at about 35 degrees elevation).

3. Parts:
Prokaryote (left):
- `prokaryote_cell_wall` - rigid wall outside the membrane; capsule-shaped shell slightly larger than the membrane; tan/light brown, semi-transparent.
- `prokaryote_capsule` - outer slimy protective layer; thicker translucent capsule shell enclosing the wall; pale yellow, ~25% opacity.
- `prokaryote_cell_membrane` - thin capsule shell just inside the wall; orange-yellow, semi-transparent.
- `prokaryote_cytoplasm` - inner capsule volume; pale light blue, translucent.
- `nucleoid_dna` - tangled loop of DNA (a single circular chromosome) in the centre, NOT enclosed by any membrane; thin dark purple tube in a squiggly closed loop.
- `plasmid` - 2-3 tiny separate circular DNA rings (torus) near the nucleoid; magenta.
- `prokaryote_ribosomes` - many tiny spheres scattered in cytoplasm (~20); dark brown, smaller than eukaryotic ribosomes.
- `flagellum` - one long thin wavy whip-like tail from one end, about 1.5x the cell length; dark grey.
- `pili` - 10-15 short thin straight hair-like spikes over the surface; light grey.
Eukaryote (right):
- `eukaryote_cell_membrane` - outer boundary; irregular rounded sphere slightly flattened; orange-yellow, semi-transparent.
- `eukaryote_cytoplasm` - interior fill; pale light blue, very translucent.
- `nucleus` - large sphere (~0.35 diameter) slightly off centre; enclosed by a double nuclear envelope; purple shell.
- `nuclear_envelope_pores` - small dark rings/holes dotted on the nuclear surface (~12); dark purple.
- `nucleolus` - dense sphere inside the nucleus (~1/3 nucleus diameter); deep violet.
- `chromatin` - thin squiggly threads inside the nucleus around the nucleolus; light purple.
- `rough_endoplasmic_reticulum` - stacked folded flattened sheets wrapping partly around the nucleus, studded with tiny dots (ribosomes); blue.
- `smooth_endoplasmic_reticulum` - network of branching tubes adjacent to the rough ER, no dots; lighter teal.
- `golgi_apparatus` - 4-5 curved stacked flattened discs (like stacked pancakes curved like a bowl) between ER and membrane, with a few small budding vesicles; gold/yellow.
- `mitochondria` - 3-4 bean-shaped capsules (~0.15 long) each cut open to show folded inner membrane (cristae) as wavy ridges; red-orange.
- `eukaryote_ribosomes` - tiny spheres free in cytoplasm (~30); dark brown.
- `lysosomes` - 3 small spheres (~0.06); green.
- `vesicles` - 5-6 tiny spheres near the Golgi and membrane; pale yellow.
- `centrioles` - pair of short cylinders at right angles near the nucleus; light green.
- `cytoskeleton` - few thin straight filaments crossing cytoplasm; pale grey, thin.

4. Internal structure: Both cells need cutaways. Cut a quarter wedge (the front-upper quadrant facing the camera) out of the eukaryote membrane and cytoplasm so organelles are visible; also cut a wedge from the nucleus to reveal nucleolus and chromatin. For the prokaryote, remove the front half of the capsule, cell wall and membrane along its long axis, showing layered edges (capsule > wall > membrane) and the interior. Mitochondria show cutaway halves revealing cristae.

5. Accuracy notes: Prokaryote has NO nucleus, NO mitochondria, NO ER/Golgi; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm. Layer order outward in prokaryote: membrane, wall, capsule. Rough ER is continuous with the nuclear envelope and carries ribosomes; smooth ER has none. Golgi sits between ER and membrane. Nucleolus is inside the nucleus. Prokaryote ribosomes smaller than eukaryote ones. Animal cell: no cell wall, no chloroplasts.

6. Keep it simple: Generic animal cell; omit chloroplasts, vacuoles, cilia. Use smooth low-detail forms, clear distinct colours, no textures. Each part a separate named object.

three_d_assets.name: Motion in One Dimension: Cart, Motion Diagram and Graphs
three_d_assets.description:
AI-generated from prompt: 1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
A review model for high-school or introductory physics students on motion in one dimension. It should connect three representations of one motion: a cart accelerating along a straight number-line track, a motion diagram of evenly timed snapshots, and the matching position-time and velocity-time graphs. Students should see that:
- displacement is a vector from the initial to the final position;
- velocity and acceleration are vectors along the line;
- equal time intervals with growing spacing mean acceleration;
- the slope of an x-t graph is velocity;
- the slope of a v-t graph is acceleration;
- the area under a v-t graph is displacement.
A small free-fall example shows that vertical motion is also 1D, with acceleration g pointing down.

2. OVERALL FORM
The scene is a tabletop diorama about 2 units across, centred at the origin, with Z up.
- The track runs along the X axis from x=-1 to x=1 at y=0, sitting on z=0.
- Two flat graph panels stand upright behind the track, side by side, at y=0.6.
- A small free-fall stand sits at the front right, near x=0.85, y=-0.55.
- Best view: from the front (negative Y), slightly above (about 25 degrees elevation), so the track, arrows and both graphs are visible together.
- Use a plain light-grey ground plate under everything.

3. PARTS
- track_position_axis: a long thin flat bar (2.0 x 0.12 x 0.03) along X, light grey, acting as a number line.
- tick_marks: thin dark-grey ticks every 0.2 units along the front edge of the track.
- origin_marker: a slightly taller black tick plus a small flat disc at x=0, labelled 0.
- positive_direction_indicator: a small white arrow at the right end of the track, pointing +X, with a '+x' plate.
- cart_initial_position: a semi-transparent pale-yellow cart (box about 0.14 x 0.1 x 0.07 with 4 small wheels) at x=-0.8.
- motion_diagram_ghosts: three faint grey translucent copies of the cart at x=-0.65, -0.4 and -0.05. These are equal time intervals; the spacing grows 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45.
- cart_final_position: a solid bright-yellow cart, same shape, at x=0.4.
- displacement_arrow: a green flat arrow just above the track at z=0.15, running from x=-0.8 to x=0.4.
- velocity_arrow_initial: a short blue arrow (length 0.1) above the initial cart at z=0.25, pointing +X.
- velocity_arrow_final: a longer blue arrow (length 0.5) above the final cart at z=0.25, pointing +X.
- acceleration_arrow: a red arrow (length 0.2) above the final cart at z=0.35, pointing +X. Same length as on every snapshot (constant acceleration).
- position_time_graph: an upright white panel (0.85 x 0.6) at x=-0.5, y=0.6, with black axes labelled t and x.
- position_time_curve: a dark-blue tube following an upward-curving parabola (concave up), rising more steeply to the right. Mark 5 dots at equal t steps matching the cart positions.
- tangent_slope_line: a short straight orange line touching the parabola at its last point, showing instantaneous velocity as slope.
- velocity_time_graph: an upright white panel, same size, at x=0.5, y=0.6, with axes labelled t and v.
- velocity_time_line: a straight blue tube from a small positive v at t=0 rising linearly; constant positive slope = acceleration.
- area_under_vt_line: a translucent green trapezoid filling the region between the line and the t-axis.
- free_fall_ball: a small red-orange sphere (radius 0.05) on a thin vertical grey post (height 0.6), with two faint ghost balls lower down and increasing spacing.
- gravity_acceleration_arrow: a red arrow pointing straight down (-Z) beside the ball, with a small 'g' plate.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
No cutaway is needed. Make the ghosts and the initial cart about 30-40% opaque so the solid final cart stands out. The area fill should be about 50% opaque so the line stays visible.

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- Cart positions must follow constant acceleration: spacings increase by a constant amount each interval (0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45).
- The displacement arrow must start exactly at the initial cart and end exactly at the final cart.
- The final velocity arrow is longer than the initial one. The acceleration arrow points in the same direction as velocity (speeding up).
- The x-t curve must be a parabola, concave up. The v-t graph must be a straight line, not curved. The v-t line starts above zero (nonzero initial velocity).
- The acceleration arrows on the ghosts are optional; if shown, they are all identical length.
- The gravity arrow points straight down. The falling-ball ghost spacing increases downward.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
- Leave out friction, forces, numbers on graph axes beyond the axis letters, and detailed cart mechanics.
- No text paragraphs; only the short labels named above.
- Use flat, clean materials and consistent colours: green = displacement, blue = velocity, red = acceleration.

three_d_assets.name: Reference Frames, Distance and Displacement
three_d_assets.description:
AI-generated from prompt: 1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
For middle and early high school physics students. The model should show that: (a) position is measured from an origin within a chosen reference frame (a coordinate system); (b) distance is the total length of the path travelled (a scalar); (c) displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to end, with a direction (a vector arrow); (d) a walking path of 3 grid squares east then 4 squares north gives a distance of 7 squares but a displacement of 5 squares (a 3-4-5 triangle); (e) motion depends on the reference frame: a passenger on a moving cart is at rest relative to the cart but moving relative to the ground observer.

2. OVERALL FORM
A flat square coordinate board with a walking route drawn on it and a small cart on a straight track along its front edge. Z is up. The board lies in the XY plane, centred at the origin, about 2 units across (-1 to +1 in X and Y). The best view is a three-quarter elevated view from the front-right (camera around (2.2, -2.4, 1.8) looking at the origin), so both the path triangle and the cart are visible. Use 1 grid square = 0.2 units.

3. PARTS
- ground_grid - thin square plate 2 x 2 x 0.02, top at z=0, light grey with thin darker grid lines every 0.2 units (lines can be a texture or thin raised strips joined into this one object).
- x_axis - red cylinder arrow (radius 0.012) along +X from the origin to x=0.95, cone tip; sits just above the grid (z=0.015). Optionally a short thin tail toward -X.
- y_axis - green cylinder arrow, same style, along +Y to y=0.95.
- z_axis - blue cylinder arrow, same style, straight up from the origin to z=0.6.
- origin_point - small white sphere (radius 0.04) at (0,0,0.02) where the three axes meet.
- ground_observer - simple stylised figure (capsule body + sphere head, ~0.25 tall), dark grey, standing at (-0.85, 0.75, 0) beside the board corner, facing the board; represents the person who owns the ground reference frame.
- start_marker - small flag: thin pole 0.18 tall with a green triangular flag, base at (-0.6, -0.4, 0).
- turning_point - small yellow disc/sphere (radius 0.035) at the corner of the route (0.0, -0.4, 0.02).
- end_marker - same flag style with a checkered or red flag, base at (0.0, 0.4, 0).
- path_leg_east - orange flattened tube or strip (width ~0.035) lying on the grid from (-0.6,-0.4) to (0.0,-0.4); length 0.6 = 3 squares. Add small chevrons or a tiny arrowhead showing direction east.
- path_leg_north - same orange strip from (0.0,-0.4) to (0.0,0.4); length 0.8 = 4 squares, arrowhead pointing north.
- displacement_arrow - bold purple 3D arrow (shaft radius 0.022, cone head) floating slightly higher (z=0.06) from the start point (-0.6,-0.4) straight to the end point (0.0,0.4); length exactly 1.0 = 5 squares. Head touches the end point.
- cart_track - two thin dark grey parallel rails along X from x=-0.95 to x=0.95 at y=-0.8 and y=-0.9 (just inside the front edge), on the grid.
- moving_cart - simple blue box cart (0.35 x 0.18 x 0.1) with four small black wheels, sitting on the track centred at (0.45, -0.85, 0.07).
- cart_reference_axes - a miniature set of axes (red X, green Y, blue Z, each ~0.15 long, thinner than the main axes) fixed to the cart's top rear corner, showing the cart has its own reference frame.
- cart_passenger - small figure like the observer (~0.15 tall), light blue, standing on the cart.
- cart_velocity_arrow - cyan arrow (~0.3 long) floating above the cart at z~0.35, pointing +X, showing the cart's motion relative to the ground.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
No cutaway or transparency needed; everything is on or above the board surface. Keep the displacement arrow slightly raised so it does not merge with the grid.

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- Path legs must be exactly 0.6 and 0.8 long and perpendicular; displacement arrow exactly 1.0 long and must start at the start flag and end at the end flag (hypotenuse of the triangle).
- Path legs must connect end-to-end at the turning point with no gap.
- Start point is NOT at the origin, to show position is measured from the origin while displacement depends only on start and end.
- Axes follow the right-hand rule: X red, Y green, Z blue, meeting at the origin.
- Cart axes must be parallel to the main axes and attached to the cart.
- Separate each part into its own named object.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
No text labels, numbers, scenery, buildings or realistic people. Flat matte colours, smooth low-poly shapes. Clarity over realism.

tour.intro: The human brain is the control centre of the body, made of the large cerebrum, the cerebellum and the brainstem, plus deep structures hidden inside. This model shows the right hemisphere from the outside and its cut inner face, so we will start with the outer lobes and grooves, move down to the cerebellum and brainstem, and then explore the internal structures on the cut surface.

steps.connection: The frontal lobe is the largest lobe of the cerebrum and sits at the front, handling planning, decisions, personality and voluntary movement. It is a good starting point because the other lobes are arranged behind and below it.
This deep groove marks the back edge of the frontal lobe. The motor cortex lies just in front of it and the touch-sensing cortex just behind it, so it divides movement control from body sensation.
Behind the central sulcus is the parietal lobe, which processes touch, temperature, pain and body position. It helps you know where your body is in space.
This deep side groove runs below the frontal and parietal lobes. It separates them from the temporal lobe underneath.
Below the lateral fissure lies the thumb-shaped temporal lobe, which processes hearing and understanding language. Its inner side holds memory and emotion structures we will see later.
At the very back of the cerebrum is the occipital lobe, the smallest lobe. It contains the visual cortex, which makes sense of signals from the eyes.
Under the frontal lobe, this small bulb receives smell signals from the nose. It passes them into the brain, completing our look at the cerebrum's outer surface.

Tucked under the occipital lobe, the ridged cerebellum coordinates balance, posture and smooth movement. It works closely with the motor areas of the frontal lobe and connects to the brainstem in front of it.
The midbrain is the top part of the brainstem, joining the thalamus above to the pons below. It handles visual and hearing reflexes and helps control eye movements.
Below the midbrain, the bulging pons relays signals between the cerebrum and the cerebellum behind it. It also helps regulate breathing and sleep.
The medulla is the narrowing bottom of the brainstem, below the pons. It automatically controls life-support functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.
The spinal cord continues down from the medulla. It carries nerve messages between the brain and the rest of the body.
Now on the cut inner face, the arched corpus callosum is a thick band of nerve fibres. It links the left and right hemispheres so they can share information.
Just below the corpus callosum lies this cavity filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid cushions the brain and helps carry away waste.
Below the ventricle and on top of the brainstem sits the thalamus, the brain's main relay station. It sends incoming sensory signals to the correct lobes of the cortex.
Just below and in front of the thalamus, the small hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep. It also directs the pituitary gland hanging beneath it.
Hanging on a stalk below the hypothalamus, this pea-sized 'master gland' releases hormones that control growth and other glands. It links the nervous system to the hormone system.
Deep in the inner temporal lobe, the curved hippocampus is essential for forming new memories and finding your way around. It is part of the brain's memory and emotion system.
Just in front of the hippocampus, the almond-shaped amygdala processes emotions, especially fear. Working with the hippocampus, it links emotions to memories.

parts.description: The narrowing lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. It controls vital automatic functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.

parts.label: Spinal Cord (cut)
parts.description: The start of the spinal cord, shown cut off below the medulla. It carries nerve signals between the brain and the rest of the body.

parts.name: thalamus
parts.label: Thalamus
parts.description: An egg-shaped mass at the centre of the brain, on top of the brainstem. It is the main relay station that sends sensory signals on to the correct areas of the cortex.

parts.name: hypothalamus
parts.label: Hypothalamus
parts.description: A small region just below and in front of the thalamus. It controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep, and it directs the pituitary gland.

parts.name: pituitary_gland
parts.label: Pituitary Gland
parts.description: A pea-sized gland hanging on a thin stalk below the hypothalamus. Often called the 'master gland', it releases hormones that control growth and other glands.

parts.name: corpus_callosum
parts.label: Corpus Callosum
parts.description: A thick, arched band of white nerve fibres above the thalamus and ventricle. It connects the left and right hemispheres so they can share information.

parts.description: A curved, seahorse-shaped structure deep in the inner temporal lobe. It is essential for forming new memories and for spatial navigation.

parts.name: amygdala
parts.label: Amygdala
parts.description: A small almond-shaped cluster just in front of the hippocampus. It processes emotions, especially fear, and links emotions to memories.

parts.name: olfactory_bulb
parts.label: Olfactory Bulb
parts.description: A thin rod with a swollen tip on the underside of the frontal lobe, pointing forward. It receives smell signals from the nose and passes them to the brain.

frontal_lobe.fact: In 1848, railway worker Phineas Gage survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe; friends reported his personality changed afterwards, an early clue that the frontal lobe shapes behaviour.
frontal_lobe.analogy: The frontal lobe is like the CEO of a company: it gathers reports from other departments, makes plans, decides what to do, and gives the orders that get things moving.
frontal_lobe.summary: The frontal lobe is the largest of the four lobes of the cerebrum, sitting at the front of each hemisphere behind the forehead. It is often called the brain's control centre because it plans, makes decisions, controls impulses, shapes personality and starts voluntary movements.
frontal_lobe.function: The front part, the prefrontal cortex, handles executive functions: planning ahead, solving problems, focusing attention, holding information in working memory and controlling impulses. It also plays a big role in personality and social behaviour. The primary motor cortex at the back of the lobe sends signals down through the brainstem and spinal cord to make skeletal muscles move, with each region of the strip controlling a different body part. Because the nerve pathways cross over, the right frontal lobe mainly controls muscles on the left side of the body. Broca's area, usually in the left frontal lobe, helps turn thoughts into spoken words.
frontal_lobe.structure: The frontal lobe takes up roughly one third of each cerebral hemisphere, stretching from the frontal pole at the front back to the central sulcus, and down to the lateral fissure on its side. Like the rest of the cortex, its surface is folded into ridges (gyri) and grooves (sulci), with an outer layer of grey matter (nerve cell bodies) over white matter (nerve fibres). Its rear strip, the precentral gyrus, is the primary motor cortex. On the left side in most people it also contains Broca's area, which is involved in producing speech.

connections.relationship: The central sulcus forms the back boundary of the frontal lobe; the motor cortex lies just in front of it, while the touch-sensing cortex lies just behind it.
The parietal lobe sits behind the frontal lobe and sends it information about touch and body position, so the frontal lobe can plan and adjust movements accurately.
This band of fibres links the frontal lobes of the two hemispheres so they can share information and coordinate movement and thinking.
The frontal lobe decides on and starts movements, while the cerebellum fine-tunes their timing, balance and smoothness.

frontal_lobe.check_answer: The primary motor cortex, a strip (the precentral gyrus) at the back of the frontal lobe, just in front of the central sulcus.
frontal_lobe.misconception: Many people think the frontal lobe is fully mature by the early teenage years. In fact, the prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain areas to finish developing, with changes continuing into the mid-twenties, which helps explain why impulse control keeps improving through adolescence.

tour.intro: A compound light microscope uses light and two sets of lenses to make tiny, see-through specimens look much larger. In this tour we will start with the parts that hold the microscope steady, follow the light from the lamp up through the specimen and lenses, and finish at the eyepiece where you see the magnified image.

steps.connection: The heavy base keeps the whole microscope stable so the image does not shake. It also houses the light source that starts the light path.
The arm rises from the base and connects it to the stage and body tube, holding all the optical parts in line. It is also the safe place to grip when carrying the microscope.
Built into the base, the illuminator shines light straight upward. Without this light there would be nothing passing through the specimen to form an image.
The stage is the flat platform above the light source where the slide sits. Its central aperture lets the upward light pass through to the specimen.
The stage clips hold the slide firmly on the stage. This keeps the specimen still and centred over the aperture so it stays in view.
The thin, clear slide carries the specimen and sits under the clips. Because glass is transparent, light from below passes through it easily.
The specimen is the thin, translucent sample we want to study. Light passing through it picks up the pattern of its details, which the lenses then magnify.
Just above the slide, the objective housing holds the objective lens at the right position close to the specimen. Here it is cut open to reveal the lens inside.
The objective lens collects light that has passed through the specimen and makes the first magnified image. This image is sent up into the body tube.
The body tube keeps the objective and eyepiece the correct distance apart so the image is formed in the right place. Light from the objective travels up inside it toward the eyepiece.
At the top of the body tube, the eyepiece housing holds the eyepiece lens and is where you place your eye. It is the final stop of the light inside the microscope.
The eyepiece lens magnifies the objective's image a second time. Total magnification equals the objective magnification multiplied by the eyepiece magnification, for example 10x times 40x gives 400x.

The glowing beam ties the whole system together, showing light travelling from the source, through the stage aperture, slide and specimen, through the objective and body tube, and out of the eyepiece to your eye. Every part we have seen either supports, holds or shapes this path.
