tour.intro: All living things are made of cells, and every cell is one of two basic types: prokaryotic, like this small rod-shaped bacterium on the left, or eukaryotic, like the larger animal cell on the right. This tour first works through the bacterium from the outside in, then explores the animal cell, so you can see what both share (membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA) and what only eukaryotes have: a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

steps.connection: The stand holds both cells side by side so you can compare them directly. Notice how much smaller the bacterium is; in real life the difference is even bigger, about 10 to 100 times.

Starting outside the bacterium, the slimy capsule is its outermost layer. It protects the cell and helps it stick to surfaces, and it is a feature found only in some prokaryotes, never in animal cells.
These short hairs stick out through the capsule and let the bacterium attach to surfaces and other cells. Some pili even pass DNA between bacteria.
The long whip-like tail spins like a propeller to drive the bacterium through liquid. Like the pili, it is a surface structure that helps the prokaryote interact with its surroundings.
Just inside the capsule, the rigid peptidoglycan wall gives the bacterium its rod shape and stops it bursting. Animal cells lack a cell wall, which is one clear difference between these two cells.
Under the wall lies the cell membrane, which controls what enters and leaves. This is a structure both cell types share.
Inside the membrane is the cytoplasm, where the cell's reactions happen. Because prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, everything else in the bacterium floats freely in this fluid.
The bacterium's single circular chromosome sits in the nucleoid region with no membrane around it. This lack of a nucleus is the defining feature of a prokaryote.
Alongside the main chromosome are small extra DNA rings called plasmids. They can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance and be shared between bacteria.
These tiny 70S ribosomes read the DNA's instructions to build proteins. Both cell types have ribosomes, but prokaryotic ones are smaller than eukaryotic ones.

Moving to the animal cell, its flexible membrane is the outermost layer because animal cells have no wall or capsule. It does the same job as the bacterium's membrane, controlling what goes in and out.
The cytoplasm fills the much larger eukaryotic cell, but unlike the bacterium's, it holds many separate membrane-bound organelles. A quarter is cut away to reveal them.
A network of protein filaments runs through the cytoplasm, giving the cell its shape and holding organelles in place. It also acts as tracks for moving materials around this large cell.
The nucleus is the key feature that makes a cell eukaryotic: its DNA is enclosed inside a double membrane. Compare this with the bacterium's nucleoid, which has no membrane at all.
Pores in the nuclear envelope let RNA and proteins move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. They connect the cell's genetic instructions to the protein-making machinery outside.

Inside the nucleus, the DNA is wound around proteins as loose chromatin threads. Unlike the single circular bacterial chromosome, eukaryotic DNA is split into several linear chromosomes that coil up before division.
The dense nucleolus makes the parts of ribosomes. These parts leave through the nuclear pores to form ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Free 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm make proteins for the cell's own use. They are larger than the 70S ribosomes in the bacterium.
Joined to the nuclear envelope, the rough ER is studded with ribosomes and makes and folds proteins for export or for membranes. It is the start of the cell's protein-processing pathway.
The smooth ER branches from the rough ER but has no ribosomes. It makes lipids, breaks down toxins and stores calcium.
Proteins from the ER travel to the Golgi, which modifies, sorts and packages them. It is the cell's dispatch centre.
Vesicles bud off the Golgi and carry materials to the cell membrane and other parts of the cell. They complete the delivery route that starts at the ER.
Lysosomes are sacs of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles, food and microbes. Keeping these enzymes inside a membrane is only possible in cells with membrane-bound compartments.

Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP through cellular respiration, using their folded inner membranes. Bacteria have no mitochondria and carry out respiration using their cell membrane instead.

Near the nucleus, a pair of centrioles helps organise spindle fibres when the animal cell divides. This completes the picture of a eukaryotic cell full of specialised parts that the simpler prokaryote does without.

parts.name: display_base
parts.label: Display Base
parts.description: Light-grey oval stand that holds the two cells side by side. It is not part of either cell.

parts.name: prokaryote_capsule
parts.label: Capsule (Prokaryote)
parts.description: Slimy outer layer that surrounds the cell wall of many bacteria. It protects the cell from drying out and from the host's immune cells, and helps it stick to surfaces.

parts.name: prokaryote_cell_wall
parts.label: Cell Wall (Prokaryote)
parts.description: Rigid layer just outside the cell membrane that gives the bacterium its rod shape and stops it from bursting. In bacteria it is made of peptidoglycan.

parts.name: prokaryote_cell_membrane
parts.label: Cell Membrane (Prokaryote)
parts.description: Thin lipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves the cell. The layers run from inside out: membrane, then wall, then capsule. Both cell types have a cell membrane.

parts.name: prokaryote_cytoplasm
parts.label: Cytoplasm (Prokaryote)
parts.description: Jelly-like fluid inside the membrane where the cell's chemical reactions happen. The DNA and ribosomes float directly in it because there are no membrane-bound organelles.

parts.name: nucleoid_dna
parts.label: Nucleoid (Circular DNA)
parts.description: The bacterium's single circular chromosome, coiled up in a region called the nucleoid. No membrane surrounds it, so prokaryotes have no nucleus.

parts.name: plasmid
parts.label: Plasmids
parts.description: Small extra rings of DNA separate from the main chromosome. They often carry useful genes, such as antibiotic resistance, and can be passed between bacteria.

parts.name: prokaryote_ribosomes
parts.label: Ribosomes (Prokaryote, 70S)
parts.description: Tiny structures without a membrane that build proteins. Prokaryotic ribosomes (70S) are smaller than eukaryotic ones (80S).

parts.name: flagellum
parts.label: Flagellum
parts.description: Long, whip-like tail that spins like a propeller to move the bacterium through liquid.

parts.name: pili
parts.label: Pili
parts.description: Short hair-like projections on the cell surface. Bacteria use them to attach to surfaces and to other cells, and some pili transfer DNA.

parts.name: nucleolus
parts.label: Nucleolus
parts.description: Dense region inside the nucleus where ribosome parts (rRNA) are made and put together.

parts.name: chromatin
parts.label: Chromatin
parts.description: DNA wound around proteins, spread as loose threads through the nucleus. Before the cell divides, it coils up tightly into chromosomes.

parts.name: nuclear_envelope_pores
parts.label: Nuclear Pores
parts.description: Openings in the nuclear envelope that let RNA and proteins move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.

parts.name: eukaryote_cytoplasm
parts.label: Cytoplasm (Eukaryote)
parts.description: Fluid that fills the cell between the membrane and the nucleus. The organelles are suspended in it. A quarter is cut away here so you can see inside.

parts.name: eukaryote_cell_membrane
parts.label: Cell Membrane (Eukaryote)
parts.description: Flexible outer boundary of the animal cell. It controls what goes in and out. Animal cells have no cell wall, so the membrane is the outermost layer.

parts.name: nucleus
parts.label: Nucleus
parts.description: Large organelle wrapped in a double membrane (the nuclear envelope) that holds the cell's DNA. Having a nucleus is the key feature that makes a cell eukaryotic. A wedge is cut out to show what is inside.

parts.name: rough_endoplasmic_reticulum
parts.label: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
parts.description: Folded, flattened membrane sheets that join onto the nuclear envelope. Ribosomes stud the surface, giving the rough look. It makes and folds proteins to be sent out of the cell or placed in membranes.

parts.name: smooth_endoplasmic_reticulum
parts.label: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
parts.description: Network of branching membrane tubes with no ribosomes. It makes lipids, breaks down toxins and stores calcium.

parts.name: golgi_apparatus
parts.label: Golgi Apparatus
parts.description: Stack of curved, flattened sacs between the ER and the cell membrane. It modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles that bud off its edges.

parts.name: vesicles
parts.label: Vesicles
parts.description: Tiny membrane bubbles that carry materials from the Golgi to the cell membrane and other parts of the cell.

parts.name: mitochondria
parts.label: Mitochondria
parts.description: Bean-shaped organelles with a double membrane. They release energy from food as ATP during cellular respiration. These are cut open to show the folded inner membrane (cristae).

parts.name: lysosomes
parts.label: Lysosomes
parts.description: Small sacs of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles, food particles and invading microbes.

parts.name: eukaryote_ribosomes
parts.label: Ribosomes (Eukaryote, 80S)
parts.description: Free ribosomes in the cytoplasm that make proteins the cell uses itself. They are larger than prokaryotic ribosomes.

parts.name: centrioles
parts.label: Centrioles
parts.description: A pair of short cylinders made of microtubules, set at right angles to each other near the nucleus. They help organise the spindle fibres during cell division in animal cells.

parts.name: cytoskeleton
parts.label: Cytoskeleton
parts.description: Network of protein filaments that gives the cell its shape, holds organelles in place and acts as tracks for moving vesicles.

parts.name: left_ventricle
parts.label: Left Ventricle
parts.description: The strongest chamber. It forms the pointed tip of the heart, called the apex. Its thick muscle wall pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta and out to the whole body.

parts.name: right_ventricle
parts.label: Right Ventricle
parts.description: The lower right chamber, which forms most of the front of the heart. It pumps oxygen-poor blood into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. The outer wall is see-through so you can see the septum inside.

parts.name: septum
parts.label: Septum
parts.description: The muscle wall inside the heart that separates the left side from the right side. It keeps oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood from mixing.

parts.name: right_atrium
parts.label: Right Atrium
parts.description: The upper right chamber. It collects oxygen-poor blood coming back from the body through the vena cavae, then passes it down to the right ventricle.

parts.name: left_atrium
parts.label: Left Atrium
parts.description: The upper left chamber at the back of the heart. It receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins and passes it down to the left ventricle.

parts.name: aorta
parts.label: Aorta
parts.description: The body's largest artery. It rises from the left ventricle and arches over the heart. Branches off the arch carry oxygen-rich blood to the head and arms, and the rest of the aorta runs down to supply the rest of the body.

parts.name: pulmonary_artery
parts.label: Pulmonary Artery
parts.description: This vessel leaves the right ventricle and splits into a left branch and a right branch. It carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. It is the only artery that carries oxygen-poor blood.

parts.name: superior_vena_cava
parts.label: Superior Vena Cava
parts.description: A large vein that brings oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck and arms down into the right atrium.

tour.intro: To describe motion, we first need a reference frame: a coordinate system with an origin from which every position is measured. This tour starts with the ground frame and its axes, then follows a walk of 3 squares east and 4 squares north to compare distance (7 squares) with displacement (5 squares). It ends with a moving cart to show that whether something is moving depends on the frame you measure from.

steps.connection: The board is the ground reference frame, and its 0.2-unit squares let us measure positions and lengths by counting squares. Everything else in the model is placed on or measured against this grid.
The origin is the fixed reference point of the ground frame. Every position on the grid is described as how far, and in which direction, it is from here.
Starting at the origin, the red X axis points east and gives one direction for measuring position. Points to the west have negative X values.
The green Y axis points north at right angles to X, so any point on the flat board can be located with an (x, y) pair.
The blue Z axis points up and completes a right-handed 3D coordinate system with X and Y. Curl your right-hand fingers from X toward Y and your thumb points along Z.
This person stands still beside the board and owns the ground frame. All the motion we describe next, the walk and the cart, is first judged from their point of view.
The walk begins at the green flag, at (-0.6, -0.4) in the ground frame. It is not at the origin, which shows that displacement depends only on where you start and finish.
From the start, the walker goes 3 squares (0.6 units) east, parallel to the X axis. This length is the first part of the total distance travelled.
At the yellow marker (0, -0.4), the walker turns from east to north. The two legs meet here at a right angle, forming the corner of a right triangle.
The walker then goes 4 squares (0.8 units) north, parallel to the Y axis. Adding both legs gives a total distance of 3 + 4 = 7 squares, a scalar with size but no direction.
The walk finishes at the red flag at (0, 0.4). The final position minus the starting position gives the overall change in position.

The purple arrow runs straight from start to end and is 5 squares long, the hypotenuse of the 3-4-5 triangle. Displacement is a vector with size and direction, and here it is shorter than the 7-square distance walked.
Now we turn from the walk to frames of reference. The rails are fixed to the ground frame and run along X, so the cart can only move east or west.
The blue cart rolls along the track and carries its own reference frame. That frame moves relative to the ground.
The cyan arrow shows that the ground observer sees the cart moving in the +X direction. In the cart's own frame, this velocity is zero.
These small axes are fixed to the cart and move with it, parallel to the ground axes. Positions measured with them stay the same for anything riding on the cart.

Measured with the cart's axes, the passenger is at rest. Measured from the ground observer's frame, the same passenger is moving east with the cart, which shows that motion always depends on the reference frame.

parts.name: ground_grid
parts.label: Coordinate Grid (Ground Frame)
parts.description: The flat board is the ground reference frame. Each grid square is 0.2 units, so positions and lengths can be counted in squares.

parts.name: x_axis
parts.label: X Axis (East)
parts.description: The red arrow points in the +X direction (east). Positions are measured along it from the origin, and the short tail shows negative X.

parts.name: y_axis
parts.label: Y Axis (North)
parts.description: The green arrow points in the +Y direction (north). With X and Z it forms a right-handed coordinate system.

parts.name: z_axis
parts.label: Z Axis (Up)
parts.description: The blue arrow points straight up. Under the right-hand rule, curling your fingers from X toward Y makes your thumb point along Z.

parts.name: origin_point
parts.label: Origin (0, 0, 0)
parts.description: The reference point where the axes meet. Every position is measured from here, so a position is a distance and a direction from the origin.

parts.name: ground_observer
parts.label: Ground Observer
parts.description: A person standing still beside the board. They own the ground reference frame, and to them the cart and its passenger are moving.

parts.name: start_marker
parts.label: Start Point (Green Flag)
parts.description: The walk begins here at (-0.6, -0.4). It is not at the origin, which shows that displacement depends only on the start and end points, not on where the origin is.

parts.name: end_marker
parts.label: End Point (Red Flag)
parts.description: The walk ends here at (0, 0.4). The final position minus the starting position gives the displacement.

parts.name: turning_point
parts.label: Turning Point
parts.description: The yellow marker at (0, -0.4) where the walker turns from east to north. The two path legs meet here at a right angle.

parts.name: path_leg_east
parts.label: Path Leg 1: 3 Squares East
parts.description: The first part of the walk is 0.6 units (3 squares) east. Its length counts toward the total distance travelled.

parts.name: path_leg_north
parts.label: Path Leg 2: 4 Squares North
parts.description: The second part of the walk is 0.8 units (4 squares) north. Total distance = 3 + 4 = 7 squares. Distance is a scalar, so it has size but no direction.

parts.name: displacement_arrow
parts.label: Displacement Vector
parts.description: The purple arrow runs straight from start to end and is 1.0 unit (5 squares) long, the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 triangle. Displacement is a vector, so it has both size and direction, and it is shorter than the 7-square distance walked.

parts.name: cart_track
parts.label: Cart Track
parts.description: Two straight rails along the X direction, fixed to the ground. The cart can only move east or west along them.

parts.name: moving_cart
parts.label: Moving Cart
parts.description: A blue cart on four wheels rolling along the track. It is a moving reference frame of its own.

parts.name: cart_reference_axes
parts.label: Cart Reference Frame Axes
parts.description: Small X (red), Y (green) and Z (blue) axes fixed to the cart and parallel to the ground axes. They move with the cart, so positions measured with them stay the same for anything riding on it.

parts.name: cart_passenger
parts.label: Cart Passenger
parts.description: A rider standing on the cart. Relative to the cart the passenger is at rest, but relative to the ground observer the passenger moves with the cart. Motion depends on the reference frame.

parts.name: cart_velocity_arrow
parts.label: Cart Velocity Arrow
parts.description: The cyan arrow shows the cart moving in the +X direction as seen from the ground frame. In the cart's own frame, this velocity is zero.

tour.intro: Motion in one dimension means an object moves along a single straight line, so its position at any moment is just one number. In this tour we follow a cart speeding up along a number-line track and see the same motion three ways: as arrows and snapshots on the track, as a position-time graph and as a velocity-time graph. We finish with a falling ball, which shows that vertical free fall is also one-dimensional motion.

steps.connection: The light-grey base simply holds the whole diorama together. It does not represent any physics quantity.
The track works as a number line along the x-axis, so the cart's position is always a single number. That is what makes this motion one-dimensional.
The origin at x = 0 is the reference point on the track. Every position is measured from here, with right positive and left negative.
The +x arrow sets which way counts as positive. Any velocity, displacement or acceleration pointing this way gets a positive sign.
The ticks every 0.2 units turn the track into a ruler. They let you read the cart's positions and compare the gaps between snapshots.
The see-through cart at x = -0.8 marks where the motion starts at t = 0. It is the first point we read on the number line.
The short blue arrow shows the cart is already moving slowly in the +x direction at the start. Velocity is a vector, so it has both a size and a direction along the line.

These faint copies show the cart at equal time intervals after the start. The gaps grow by the same amount each interval, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 and then 0.45, which means the cart has constant acceleration.
The solid yellow cart at x = 0.4 is the last snapshot, at the end of the fourth time interval. It completes the motion diagram that began with the initial cart.
The long blue arrow over the final cart shows a much higher velocity than at the start. Comparing it with the short initial arrow shows that the cart sped up.
The red arrow points +x, the same way as the velocity, so the cart speeds up. Its length stays the same at every snapshot because the acceleration is constant.
The green arrow runs from the initial position to the final position, giving a displacement of 0.4 - (-0.8) = +1.2. It depends only on where the motion starts and ends, not on the path in between.
Now we switch to a graph of the same motion. This panel plots the cart's position x against time t.

The five dots match the five cart positions at equal time steps, and they lie on an upward-curving parabola. The curve gets steeper because the velocity keeps increasing, just as the snapshot gaps keep growing.
The orange tangent touches the x-t curve at its last point. Its slope is the instantaneous velocity at that moment, which matches the long final velocity arrow.
This panel plots the cart's velocity v against time t. It takes the slopes from the x-t graph and shows them directly as values.
The straight line starts above zero because the cart is already moving, and it rises steadily as the cart speeds up. Its constant slope is the acceleration, matching the unchanging red arrow.
The green trapezoid under the v-t line has an area equal to the cart's displacement. This links back to the green displacement arrow of +1.2 on the track.

A ball dropped beside the post is captured at equal time intervals, and the gaps grow as it falls, just like the cart's snapshots. This shows that vertical free fall is also one-dimensional accelerated motion.
The red g arrow points straight down because gravity gives a constant downward acceleration of about 9.8 m/s². It plays the same role as the cart's red acceleration arrow, but along a vertical line.

parts.name: ground_plate
parts.label: Ground Plate
parts.description: A plain light-grey base that holds the whole diorama. It is only there for support and does not stand for any physics quantity.

parts.name: track_position_axis
parts.label: Track / Position Axis
parts.description: A straight track that works as a number line along the x-axis, from x = -1 to x = +1. The cart's position at any moment is a single number on this line, so the motion is one-dimensional.

parts.name: tick_marks
parts.label: Tick Marks
parts.description: Evenly spaced marks every 0.2 units along the front edge of the track. They let you read positions and compare the distances between snapshots.

parts.name: origin_marker
parts.label: Origin (x = 0)
parts.description: The reference point labelled 0. Positions are measured from here: positive to the right, negative to the left.

parts.name: positive_direction_indicator
parts.label: Positive Direction (+x)
parts.description: The white arrow and '+x' plate set +x as the positive direction. Any vector pointing this way has a positive sign.

parts.name: cart_initial_position
parts.label: Cart – Initial Position
parts.description: A see-through cart at x = -0.8 showing where the motion starts (t = 0). The displacement arrow begins here.

parts.name: motion_diagram_ghosts
parts.label: Motion Diagram Snapshots
parts.description: Faint copies of the cart at x = -0.65, -0.4 and -0.05, taken at equal time intervals. Including the initial and final carts, the gaps grow by 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 and 0.45. Gaps that grow by the same amount each interval mean constant acceleration.

parts.name: cart_final_position
parts.label: Cart – Final Position
parts.description: The solid yellow cart at x = 0.4, its position at the end of the fourth time interval. The displacement arrow ends here.

parts.name: displacement_arrow
parts.label: Displacement Vector
parts.description: A green arrow from the initial position (-0.8) to the final position (0.4). Displacement = x_final - x_initial = +1.2. It depends only on where the motion starts and ends.

parts.name: velocity_arrow_initial
parts.label: Initial Velocity
parts.description: A short blue arrow showing that the cart is already moving slowly in the +x direction at the start. A shorter arrow means a lower speed.

parts.name: velocity_arrow_final
parts.label: Final Velocity
parts.description: A longer blue arrow showing the cart's higher velocity at the end. It is longer than the initial arrow because the cart sped up.

parts.name: acceleration_arrow
parts.label: Acceleration Vector
parts.description: A red arrow pointing +x, the same direction as the velocity, so the cart speeds up. Its length is the same throughout the motion because the acceleration is constant.

parts.name: position_time_graph
parts.label: Position–Time (x–t) Graph
parts.description: A panel with a time axis (t) and a position axis (x). It shows how the cart's position changes over time.

parts.name: velocity_time_graph
parts.label: Velocity–Time (v–t) Graph
parts.description: A panel with a time axis (t) and a velocity axis (v). It shows how the cart's velocity changes over time.

parts.name: velocity_time_line
parts.label: v–t Line
parts.description: A straight line that starts above zero (the cart is already moving) and rises steadily. Its constant slope is the acceleration.

parts.name: area_under_vt_line
parts.label: Area Under v–t Line (Displacement)
parts.description: The green trapezoid between the v–t line and the time axis. Its area equals the cart's displacement, which matches the green arrow on the track.

parts.name: free_fall_ball
parts.label: Free-Fall Ball and Stand
parts.description: A ball released from a vertical post, with faint copies lower down taken at equal time intervals. The gaps grow as it falls, showing that vertical free fall is also one-dimensional accelerated motion.

parts.name: gravity_acceleration_arrow
parts.label: Gravitational Acceleration (g)
parts.description: A red arrow pointing straight down, labelled g. In free fall the acceleration is constant and always points downward, about 9.8 m/s².

parts.name: position_time_curve
parts.label: x–t Curve (Parabola)
parts.description: An upward-curving parabola for constant acceleration. The five dots at equal time steps match the five cart positions. The curve gets steeper because the velocity keeps increasing.

parts.name: tangent_slope_line
parts.label: Tangent Line (Instantaneous Velocity)
parts.description: An orange line touching the x–t curve at its last point. Its slope is the cart's instantaneous velocity at that moment.

three_d_prompt_drafts.subject: bio
three_d_prompt_drafts.title: Human Body: Major Internal Organs
three_d_prompt_drafts.prompt:
1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
An interactive model of the human body for grade 9 biology students. Students should see where the major organs sit inside the body and how they group into systems: nervous (brain, spinal cord), respiratory (trachea, lungs, diaphragm), circulatory (heart, aorta, vena cava), digestive (esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, small and large intestine), excretory/urinary (kidneys, ureters, bladder) and lymphatic (spleen). Spatial relationships matter more than fine detail.

2. OVERALL FORM
A standing, gender-neutral human figure, front-facing toward -Y, Z up, arms slightly away from the sides, legs simplified. The whole figure is about 2 units tall, centred at the origin. Head top near Z=+1.0, feet near Z=-1.0. Best view: front, slightly from above and rotated about 20 degrees. The body is a transparent shell so organs are visible inside. Anatomical left is the figure's left, at +X when the figure faces -Y.

3. PARTS
- body_outline: smooth, low-detail human silhouette (head, neck, torso, arms, legs). Pale skin tone, about 80% transparent, no facial detail beyond a simple head shape. Encloses everything.
- brain: rounded, slightly wrinkled ellipsoid filling the upper head. Pink-beige.
- spinal_cord: thin cylinder running from the base of the brain down the back of the neck and torso to about waist level. Behind all the torso organs. Pale yellow-white.
- trachea: ringed tube about 0.03 wide from the throat down to the top of the chest, splitting into two short bronchi into the lungs. Light grey-blue.
- right_lung: large spongy cone on the figure's right side of the chest (-X). It has 3 lobes indicated by shallow grooves. Salmon pink.
- left_lung: same as the right lung but slightly smaller with a notch for the heart. It has 2 lobes. Salmon pink.
- heart: fist-sized rounded cone in the chest centre, between the lungs and tilted with its apex pointing down-left (+X). Red.
- aorta: thick red tube arching up from the top of the heart, curving back and left, then running down in front of the spine into the abdomen. Bright red.
- vena_cava: thick blue tube running vertically just right of the spine (-X) into the right side of the heart. Blue.
- diaphragm: thin dome-shaped sheet under the lungs and heart, separating the chest from the abdomen. Dark red-brown muscle colour.
- esophagus: thin tube behind the trachea, running down through the diaphragm into the stomach. Pale pink.
- stomach: J-shaped bean sac in the upper abdomen on the figure's left (+X), just below the diaphragm. Pink-orange.
- liver: large wedge-shaped organ, the biggest in the abdomen, on the figure's right (-X) under the diaphragm, extending partly across the midline. Dark reddish-brown.
- gallbladder: small green pear-shaped sac tucked under the lower edge of the liver. Green.
- pancreas: long, flat, tapering organ lying horizontally behind and below the stomach. Pale yellow.
- spleen: small fist-shaped oval on the far left (+X) behind the stomach. Dark purple.
- small_intestine: densely coiled tube filling the central lower abdomen. Light pink.
- large_intestine: wider tube framing the small intestine like an upside-down U. It rises on the figure's right, crosses the top, descends on the left, and ends at the rectum in the centre. Tan-brown.
- right_kidney: bean shape against the back wall at waist level, right of the spine (-X), sitting slightly lower than the left kidney. Deep red-maroon.
- left_kidney: same shape as the right kidney, left of the spine (+X). Deep red-maroon.
- ureters: two thin tubes running from each kidney down to the bladder. Pale yellow.
- urinary_bladder: small rounded sac at the bottom centre of the pelvis. Yellow.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
No cutaway is needed. Make body_outline a transparent shell so every organ is visible. All organs are opaque solid meshes. Kidneys, spinal cord and pancreas sit toward the back, so from the front view they are partly behind the other organs. This is correct, and students rotate the model to see them.

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- The heart sits slightly left of centre, with the left lung smaller than the right.
- The right lung has 3 lobes and the left lung has 2.
- The liver is on the right and is the largest internal organ. The stomach and spleen are on the left.
- The trachea is in front of the esophagus.
- The esophagus passes through the diaphragm to the stomach.
- The aorta leaves the heart. The vena cava enters the heart.
- The large intestine surrounds the small intestine.
- There are 2 kidneys and 2 ureters leading to 1 bladder.
- The diaphragm sits below the lungs and above the liver and stomach.
- The brain connects to the spinal cord.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
Leave out:
- the full skeleton, muscles, small vessels, nerves beyond the spinal cord, reproductive organs, glands such as the thyroid and adrenals, and the appendix
- facial features, hair, fingers and toes
Use smooth, low-poly-friendly shapes and clear distinct colours. Make each organ a separate named object. Clarity matters more than realism.

parts.name: body_outline
parts.label: Body Outline (Skin)
parts.description: The outer surface of the body, shown see-through here. Skin protects the internal organs and helps control body temperature.

parts.name: brain
parts.label: Brain
parts.description: The control centre of the nervous system. It processes information from the senses and sends signals that control movement, thought and body functions.

parts.name: spinal_cord
parts.label: Spinal Cord
parts.description: A thick bundle of nerves running from the brain down the back, protected by the spine. It carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body.

parts.name: trachea
parts.label: Trachea (Windpipe)
parts.description: A tube held open by rings of cartilage that carries air from the throat to the lungs. At the bottom it splits into two bronchi.

parts.name: right_lung
parts.label: Right Lung
parts.description: One of the two organs where gas exchange happens: oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. The right lung has three lobes.

parts.name: left_lung
parts.label: Left Lung
parts.description: The left lung has only two lobes and is slightly smaller than the right lung, leaving room for the heart.

parts.name: heart
parts.label: Heart
parts.description: A muscular pump that pushes blood around the body. It sits between the lungs, tilted slightly to the left.

parts.name: aorta
parts.label: Aorta
parts.description: The body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart to the rest of the body.

parts.name: vena_cava
parts.label: Vena Cava
parts.description: The largest vein. It returns oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right side of the heart.

parts.name: diaphragm
parts.label: Diaphragm
parts.description: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, air is drawn into the lungs.

parts.name: esophagus
parts.label: Esophagus
parts.description: A muscular tube that moves swallowed food from the throat to the stomach using wave-like contractions called peristalsis.

parts.name: stomach
parts.label: Stomach
parts.description: A stretchy muscular sac that churns food and mixes it with acid and enzymes to begin digesting proteins.

parts.name: liver
parts.label: Liver
parts.description: The largest internal organ. It makes bile to help digest fats, stores nutrients and removes toxins from the blood.

parts.name: gallbladder
parts.label: Gallbladder
parts.description: A small sac under the liver that stores bile and releases it into the small intestine.

parts.name: pancreas
parts.label: Pancreas
parts.description: A gland behind the stomach that releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine. It also makes the hormones insulin and glucagon, which control blood sugar.

parts.name: spleen
parts.label: Spleen
parts.description: An organ on the left side that filters the blood, removes old red blood cells and helps the immune system fight infection.

parts.name: small_intestine
parts.label: Small Intestine
parts.description: A long coiled tube where most digestion finishes and nutrients are absorbed into the blood.

parts.name: large_intestine
parts.label: Large Intestine
parts.description: A wider tube that absorbs water from undigested material and forms feces, which leave the body through the rectum.

parts.name: right_kidney
parts.label: Right Kidney
parts.description: A bean-shaped organ that filters wastes and extra water from the blood to make urine. It sits slightly lower than the left kidney because the liver is above it.

parts.name: left_kidney
parts.label: Left Kidney
parts.description: The second kidney. It also filters blood and helps balance water and salts in the body.

parts.name: ureters
parts.label: Ureters
parts.description: Two thin tubes that carry urine from the kidneys down to the bladder.

parts.name: urinary_bladder
parts.label: Urinary Bladder
parts.description: A stretchy sac in the pelvis that stores urine until it is released from the body.

three_d_prompt_drafts.title: The Human Brain: Major Regions and Structures
three_d_prompt_drafts.prompt:
1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
An interactive model for middle to high school biology students. They should identify the main external regions of the brain (the four cerebral lobes, cerebellum, brainstem) and key internal structures (corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, pituitary gland, ventricles). They should also understand where each part sits relative to the others. Each region is a separate, clickable mesh with a distinct colour.

2. OVERALL FORM
Build a stylised adult human brain, about 2 units long front-to-back (Y axis), centred at the origin, with Z up. The front (frontal pole) points toward -Y. The left hemisphere is on -X.
- Right hemisphere: complete, with the external lobes.
- Left hemisphere: shown as a midsagittal cutaway. The left hemisphere is removed so the flat medial (inner) face of the right hemisphere faces -X and the internal midline structures are exposed. Put the internal midline structures on this cut face.
The best view is from the front-left at an elevation of about 20 degrees, so students see the lateral lobes and the cut medial face. Overall proportions: length 2.0, height about 1.5, width of the single hemisphere about 0.75. Give the cortex a gently bumpy surface. Suggest gyri and sulci with displacement or shallow grooves, but keep the lobes as clean separate shapes.

3. PARTS
- frontal_lobe - The front of the cerebrum, extending back to the central sulcus at about the midpoint of the top. It is the largest lobe, about 1/3 of the hemisphere. Colour: blue.
- parietal_lobe - Sits behind the frontal lobe and above the temporal lobe, running from the central sulcus to the parieto-occipital sulcus. Colour: yellow.
- temporal_lobe - The lower side lobe, below the lateral (Sylvian) fissure. Shaped like a thumb pointing forward. Colour: green.
- occipital_lobe - The rear pole of the cerebrum, the smallest lobe. Colour: orange.
- cerebellum - A rounded, finely ridged structure with horizontal folia grooves. It sits under the occipital lobe at the back, behind the brainstem. About 1/4 of the brain's length. Colour: purple.
- brainstem - A tapered column below the centre of the brain, angled slightly forward. Divide it into three stacked segments:
  - midbrain (top, short, light pink)
  - pons (middle, bulging forward, salmon)
  - medulla_oblongata (bottom, narrowing, rose)
- spinal_cord_stub - A short cylinder continuing below the medulla, cut off. Colour: pale grey.
- corpus_callosum - On the cut medial face: a thick C-shaped (arched) band of white fibres above the thalamus. It spans about the middle half of the brain's length. Colour: white.
- lateral_ventricle - A thin, curved, fluid-filled cavity just below the corpus callosum, visible on the cut face. Colour: light cyan, semi-transparent.
- thalamus - An egg-shaped mass in the centre, below the corpus callosum and on top of the brainstem. Colour: teal.
- hypothalamus - A small region just below and in front of the thalamus. Colour: magenta.
- pituitary_gland - A pea-sized ball hanging on a thin stalk below the hypothalamus. Colour: red.
- hippocampus - A curved, seahorse-like tube deep in the medial temporal lobe, below and behind the thalamus. Show it as slightly protruding on the cut face. Colour: gold.
- amygdala - A small almond shape just in front of the hippocampus tip. Colour: dark red.
- olfactory_bulb - A thin rod with a bulb end under the frontal lobe, pointing forward. Colour: light green.
- central_sulcus - A visible groove separating the frontal and parietal lobes. Model it as a thin dark curved strip mesh. Colour: dark grey.
- lateral_fissure - A deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. Model it as a dark strip. Colour: dark grey.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
Use the midsagittal cut described above. No transparent shell is needed. The cut face of the cortex should be a slightly darker tone of each lobe's colour, to suggest grey matter, with lighter interior. The deep structures sit flush with or slightly raised from the cut plane:
- thalamus
- hypothalamus
- corpus callosum
- ventricle
- hippocampus
- amygdala

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- Four lobes per hemisphere.
- The cerebellum is posterior and inferior, never above the cerebrum.
- The brainstem connects the cerebrum (via the midbrain at the thalamus) to the spinal cord.
- The pons bulges anteriorly.
- The corpus callosum is above the thalamus and ventricle.
- The pituitary is below the hypothalamus, connected by a stalk.
- The hippocampus lies within the temporal lobe, medial side.
- The olfactory bulb is on the underside of the frontal lobe.
- The cerebrum is by far the largest part, about 80-85% of the volume.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
Omit the following:
- blood vessels
- meninges
- cranial nerves (other than the olfactory bulb)
- basal ganglia
- detailed individual gyri names
- skull
Use smooth stylised shapes and flat, clearly distinct colours, with no photorealistic textures. Name each mesh object exactly as the part names above.

parts.name: frontal_lobe
parts.label: Frontal Lobe
parts.description: The front part of the cerebrum. It controls planning, decision-making, personality, speech production and voluntary movement.

parts.name: parietal_lobe
parts.label: Parietal Lobe
parts.description: Sits behind the frontal lobe. It processes touch, temperature, pain and body position, and helps with spatial awareness.

parts.name: temporal_lobe
parts.label: Temporal Lobe
parts.description: The lower side lobe near the ears. It handles hearing, language understanding and some memory.

parts.name: occipital_lobe
parts.label: Occipital Lobe
parts.description: The back of the cerebrum. It is the main center for processing vision.

parts.name: cerebellum
parts.label: Cerebellum
parts.description: The 'little brain' under the back of the cerebrum. It coordinates balance, posture and smooth, precise movements.

parts.name: midbrain
parts.label: Midbrain
parts.description: The top part of the brainstem. It relays visual and auditory signals and helps control eye movements.

parts.name: pons
parts.label: Pons
parts.description: The bulging middle part of the brainstem. It relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate breathing and sleep.

parts.name: medulla_oblongata
parts.label: Medulla Oblongata
parts.description: The lowest part of the brainstem. It controls vital automatic functions like heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure.

parts.name: spinal_cord_stub
parts.label: Spinal Cord
parts.description: Continues down from the medulla. It carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body.

parts.name: corpus_callosum
parts.label: Corpus Callosum
parts.description: A thick band of nerve fibres connecting the left and right hemispheres. It lets the two halves of the brain share information.

parts.name: lateral_ventricle
parts.label: Lateral Ventricle
parts.description: A fluid-filled space inside the brain. It contains cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions and nourishes the brain.

parts.name: thalamus
parts.label: Thalamus
parts.description: A relay station deep in the brain. It sorts and passes most sensory information to the correct areas of the cortex.

parts.name: hypothalamus
parts.label: Hypothalamus
parts.description: A small region below the thalamus. It regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep, and controls the pituitary gland.

parts.name: pituitary_gland
parts.label: Pituitary Gland
parts.description: A pea-sized gland hanging below the hypothalamus. It releases hormones that control growth and many other glands.

parts.name: hippocampus
parts.label: Hippocampus
parts.description: A curved structure in the temporal lobe. It is essential for forming new memories.

parts.name: amygdala
parts.label: Amygdala
parts.description: A small almond-shaped structure in front of the hippocampus. It processes emotions, especially fear.

parts.name: olfactory_bulb
parts.label: Olfactory Bulb
parts.description: Lies under the frontal lobe. It receives smell signals from the nose.

parts.name: central_sulcus
parts.label: Central Sulcus
parts.description: A deep groove separating the frontal and parietal lobes. The movement and touch areas of the cortex lie on either side of it.

parts.name: lateral_fissure
parts.label: Lateral Fissure
parts.description: A deep groove that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes above it.

three_d_prompt_drafts.title: Compound Light Microscope: How Cells Are Studied
three_d_prompt_drafts.prompt:
1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
An interactive model of a compound light microscope, the main tool for studying cells, for middle and high school biology students. Students should learn how light travels from the illuminator up through the condenser, the specimen on the slide, an objective lens and the eyepiece, which together magnify the image. Total magnification equals eyepiece power times objective power (for example 10x times 40x = 400x). Students should also learn which parts hold the specimen, change magnification and adjust focus, and that coarse focus is used first and fine focus last.

2. OVERALL FORM
A classic upright student compound microscope seen from the side, Z up, centred at the origin and about 2 units tall. The C-shaped arm is at the back (-Y side) and the stage and optics face forward (+Y). The base sits flat at the bottom. The best view is a 3/4 front-right view from slightly above, which shows the stage, the objectives and the focus knobs on the right side. Use clean, slightly stylised geometry with smooth bevels.

3. PARTS
- base - heavy flat horseshoe or rounded rectangular slab, about 1.0 x 0.7 x 0.12 units, at the bottom. Dark charcoal grey.
- arm - thick curved C-shaped column rising from the back of the base to support the head, about 1.5 units tall. Off-white or cream.
- light_source - small glowing disc lamp set into the top of the base, directly under the stage opening. Warm yellow emissive.
- diaphragm - thin disc about 0.25 wide with a small radial lever, just under the stage and above the condenser. Medium grey. It controls the amount of light.
- condenser_lens - short cylinder under the stage opening holding a pale blue glass lens on top. Silver body.
- stage - flat square platform about 0.6 x 0.6 x 0.05, mounted on the arm at mid-height, with a round hole (aperture) in the centre. Black.
- stage_clips - two thin metal spring clips on the stage top, one on each side of the slide. Silver.
- glass_slide - thin transparent rectangle about 0.45 x 0.15 x 0.01 lying on the stage across the aperture. Pale transparent glass.
- specimen - small square coverslip area at the slide centre containing a few tiny stained cells (flattened ellipses with dark dots for nuclei). Pink-purple stain.
- revolving_nosepiece - rotating dome-shaped turret under the front of the head, angled slightly. Silver.
- objective_low_power - shortest objective lens (4x) screwed into the nosepiece. Silver with a red ring.
- objective_medium_power - medium length objective (10x). Silver with a yellow ring.
- objective_high_power - longest objective (40x). Silver with a blue ring. Its tip points down at the specimen and sits close above the slide.
- body_tube - straight tube connecting the nosepiece up to the eyepiece, tilted about 30-45 degrees toward the viewer (+Y). Cream.
- eyepiece - narrow cylinder at the top of the body tube with a rubber eyecup, about 0.25 long, labelled 10x. Black.
- coarse_focus_knob - large knob, about 0.25 diameter, on the right side of the arm near the stage height, with one matching knob on the left. Dark grey with ridged edges.
- fine_focus_knob - smaller knob, about 0.12 diameter, mounted coaxially outside the coarse knob on each side. Light grey.
- light_path - thin semi-transparent glowing vertical beam running from the light_source up through the condenser, the slide, the high power objective and the body tube to the eyepiece. Bright yellow at 30% opacity, following the tube angle.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
No cutaway is needed. The light_path beam should remain visible: make the body tube slightly transparent (about 40% opacity) so the beam can be seen passing through it. All other parts are solid.

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- Exactly 3 objectives on the nosepiece, and they must differ clearly in length: low is shortest, high is longest.
- The light source, diaphragm, condenser, stage aperture, specimen and active objective must align on one vertical axis.
- The eyepiece is at the top of the body tube, and the objectives point down at the stage.
- The coarse knob is larger than the fine knob, and the two are coaxial.
- The stage is below the objectives and above the condenser.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
Leave out cables, brand text, a mechanical stage, a dual eyepiece head, screws and the internal prisms. Use only short magnification labels if text is easy to add; otherwise use the coloured rings. Prioritise clear separate meshes with distinct colours so each part is easy to click.

parts.name: base
parts.label: Base
parts.description: The heavy bottom of the microscope that keeps it steady. It also houses the light source.

parts.name: arm
parts.label: Arm
parts.description: The curved frame that connects the base to the head. Always carry the microscope by the arm, with a hand under the base.

parts.name: light_source
parts.label: Light Source (Illuminator)
parts.description: A lamp that shines light up through the specimen. Light microscopes form images using visible light passing through thin samples.

parts.name: diaphragm
parts.label: Diaphragm
parts.description: An adjustable opening that controls how much light reaches the specimen. Less light often increases contrast in clear cells.

parts.name: condenser_lens
parts.label: Condenser Lens
parts.description: Focuses light from the lamp into a bright cone onto the specimen. This gives a sharper, evenly lit image.

parts.name: stage
parts.label: Stage
parts.description: The flat platform where the slide sits. Light passes up through the hole in its centre.

parts.name: stage_clips
parts.label: Stage Clips
parts.description: Metal clips that hold the slide in place so it does not slide while you observe.

parts.name: glass_slide
parts.label: Glass Slide
parts.description: A thin piece of glass that holds the specimen. A coverslip is placed on top to flatten and protect the sample.

parts.name: specimen
parts.label: Specimen (Stained Cells)
parts.description: A thin sample of cells, often stained with dyes so structures such as the nucleus show up. Most cells are too small to see without magnification.

parts.name: revolving_nosepiece
parts.label: Revolving Nosepiece
parts.description: A rotating turret that holds the objective lenses. Turn it to switch between magnifications.

parts.name: objective_low_power
parts.label: Low Power Objective (4x)
parts.description: The shortest objective, used first to find the specimen. It shows a wide field of view at low magnification.

parts.name: objective_medium_power
parts.label: Medium Power Objective (10x)
parts.description: A medium-strength lens. Combined with a 10x eyepiece, it gives 100x total magnification.

parts.name: objective_high_power
parts.label: High Power Objective (40x)
parts.description: The longest objective, giving 400x total magnification with a 10x eyepiece. Use only the fine focus with this lens to avoid breaking the slide.

parts.name: body_tube
parts.label: Body Tube
parts.description: The tube that carries light from the objective lens up to the eyepiece. It keeps the lenses the correct distance apart.

parts.name: eyepiece
parts.label: Eyepiece (Ocular Lens)
parts.description: The lens you look through, usually 10x. Total magnification equals the eyepiece power times the objective power.

parts.name: coarse_focus_knob
parts.label: Coarse Focus Knob
parts.description: The large knob that moves the stage up or down quickly to bring the specimen roughly into focus. Use it only with the low power objective.

parts.name: fine_focus_knob
parts.label: Fine Focus Knob
parts.description: The small knob that makes tiny focus adjustments for a sharp image. Use it at higher magnifications.

parts.name: light_path
parts.label: Light Path
parts.description: The route light takes: from the lamp, through the condenser, the specimen, the objective and the body tube, and out through the eyepiece to your eye. Two lenses in a row make this a compound microscope.

three_d_prompt_drafts.title: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cells
three_d_prompt_drafts.prompt:
1. Purpose and audience: Middle/high school biology students compare a prokaryotic cell (bacterium) with a eukaryotic cell (generalised animal cell) side by side. They should see that prokaryotes are much smaller and lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (their DNA sits free in a nucleoid region), while eukaryotes have a nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles. Both share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

2. Overall form: Two cells sit on a flat, light-grey oval base plate (base_plate is not a clickable teaching part; name it 'display_base'). Z is up. The whole scene is about 2 units across, centred at the origin. The eukaryotic cell is on the right (+X), a rounded blob about 1.1 units in diameter, centred near x=+0.4. The prokaryotic cell is on the left (-X), a capsule (rod) about 0.45 units long and 0.18 wide, centred near x=-0.7, lying horizontally. The size difference is deliberate but still exaggerated for visibility (real eukaryotes are ~10-100x larger); keep the prokaryote clearly much smaller. Best view: three-quarter from front-above (camera at about 35 degrees elevation).

3. Parts:
Prokaryote (left):
- `prokaryote_cell_wall` - rigid wall outside the membrane; capsule-shaped shell slightly larger than the membrane; tan/light brown, semi-transparent.
- `prokaryote_capsule` - outer slimy protective layer; thicker translucent capsule shell enclosing the wall; pale yellow, ~25% opacity.
- `prokaryote_cell_membrane` - thin capsule shell just inside the wall; orange-yellow, semi-transparent.
- `prokaryote_cytoplasm` - inner capsule volume; pale light blue, translucent.
- `nucleoid_dna` - tangled loop of DNA (a single circular chromosome) in the centre, NOT enclosed by any membrane; thin dark purple tube in a squiggly closed loop.
- `plasmid` - 2-3 tiny separate circular DNA rings (torus) near the nucleoid; magenta.
- `prokaryote_ribosomes` - many tiny spheres scattered in cytoplasm (~20); dark brown, smaller than eukaryotic ribosomes.
- `flagellum` - one long thin wavy whip-like tail from one end, about 1.5x the cell length; dark grey.
- `pili` - 10-15 short thin straight hair-like spikes over the surface; light grey.
Eukaryote (right):
- `eukaryote_cell_membrane` - outer boundary; irregular rounded sphere slightly flattened; orange-yellow, semi-transparent.
- `eukaryote_cytoplasm` - interior fill; pale light blue, very translucent.
- `nucleus` - large sphere (~0.35 diameter) slightly off centre; enclosed by a double nuclear envelope; purple shell.
- `nuclear_envelope_pores` - small dark rings/holes dotted on the nuclear surface (~12); dark purple.
- `nucleolus` - dense sphere inside the nucleus (~1/3 nucleus diameter); deep violet.
- `chromatin` - thin squiggly threads inside the nucleus around the nucleolus; light purple.
- `rough_endoplasmic_reticulum` - stacked folded flattened sheets wrapping partly around the nucleus, studded with tiny dots (ribosomes); blue.
- `smooth_endoplasmic_reticulum` - network of branching tubes adjacent to the rough ER, no dots; lighter teal.
- `golgi_apparatus` - 4-5 curved stacked flattened discs (like stacked pancakes curved like a bowl) between ER and membrane, with a few small budding vesicles; gold/yellow.
- `mitochondria` - 3-4 bean-shaped capsules (~0.15 long) each cut open to show folded inner membrane (cristae) as wavy ridges; red-orange.
- `eukaryote_ribosomes` - tiny spheres free in cytoplasm (~30); dark brown.
- `lysosomes` - 3 small spheres (~0.06); green.
- `vesicles` - 5-6 tiny spheres near the Golgi and membrane; pale yellow.
- `centrioles` - pair of short cylinders at right angles near the nucleus; light green.
- `cytoskeleton` - few thin straight filaments crossing cytoplasm; pale grey, thin.

4. Internal structure: Both cells need cutaways. Cut a quarter wedge (the front-upper quadrant facing the camera) out of the eukaryote membrane and cytoplasm so organelles are visible; also cut a wedge from the nucleus to reveal nucleolus and chromatin. For the prokaryote, remove the front half of the capsule, cell wall and membrane along its long axis, showing layered edges (capsule > wall > membrane) and the interior. Mitochondria show cutaway halves revealing cristae.

5. Accuracy notes: Prokaryote has NO nucleus, NO mitochondria, NO ER/Golgi; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm. Layer order outward in prokaryote: membrane, wall, capsule. Rough ER is continuous with the nuclear envelope and carries ribosomes; smooth ER has none. Golgi sits between ER and membrane. Nucleolus is inside the nucleus. Prokaryote ribosomes smaller than eukaryote ones. Animal cell: no cell wall, no chloroplasts.

6. Keep it simple: Generic animal cell; omit chloroplasts, vacuoles, cilia. Use smooth low-detail forms, clear distinct colours, no textures. Each part a separate named object.

parts.name: prokaryote_capsule
parts.label: Capsule
parts.description: A sticky outer layer around some bacteria. It protects the cell and helps it stick to surfaces.

parts.name: prokaryote_cell_wall
parts.label: Cell Wall (Prokaryote)
parts.description: A rigid layer outside the membrane that gives the bacterium its shape and stops it bursting.

parts.name: prokaryote_cell_membrane
parts.label: Cell Membrane (Prokaryote)
parts.description: A thin barrier that controls what enters and leaves the cell. All cells have one.

parts.name: prokaryote_cytoplasm
parts.label: Cytoplasm (Prokaryote)
parts.description: The jelly-like fluid filling the cell where chemical reactions happen.

parts.name: nucleoid_dna
parts.label: Nucleoid (DNA)
parts.description: The bacterium's single circular chromosome. It floats in the cytoplasm because prokaryotes have no nucleus.

parts.name: plasmid
parts.label: Plasmids
parts.description: Small extra rings of DNA found in bacteria. They can carry genes such as antibiotic resistance and be shared between cells.

parts.name: prokaryote_ribosomes
parts.label: Ribosomes (Prokaryote)
parts.description: Tiny structures that make proteins. Bacterial ribosomes are smaller than those in eukaryotic cells.

parts.name: flagellum
parts.label: Flagellum
parts.description: A long whip-like tail that spins to push the bacterium through liquid.

parts.name: pili
parts.label: Pili
parts.description: Short hair-like projections that help bacteria attach to surfaces and to each other.

parts.name: eukaryote_cell_membrane
parts.label: Cell Membrane (Eukaryote)
parts.description: The flexible outer boundary of the animal cell that controls movement of substances in and out.

parts.name: eukaryote_cytoplasm
parts.label: Cytoplasm (Eukaryote)
parts.description: The fluid that fills the cell and holds the organelles in place.

parts.name: nucleus
parts.label: Nucleus
parts.description: The control centre of a eukaryotic cell, holding DNA inside a double membrane. Having a nucleus is what makes a cell eukaryotic.

parts.name: nuclear_envelope_pores
parts.label: Nuclear Pores
parts.description: Openings in the nuclear envelope that let materials like RNA move between the nucleus and cytoplasm.

parts.name: nucleolus
parts.label: Nucleolus
parts.description: A dense region inside the nucleus where ribosomes are made.

parts.name: chromatin
parts.label: Chromatin
parts.description: DNA wrapped around proteins inside the nucleus. It coils up into chromosomes when the cell divides.

parts.name: rough_endoplasmic_reticulum
parts.label: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
parts.description: Folded membranes covered in ribosomes, connected to the nucleus. It makes and transports proteins.

parts.name: smooth_endoplasmic_reticulum
parts.label: Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
parts.description: A network of tubes without ribosomes that makes lipids and helps detoxify substances.

parts.name: golgi_apparatus
parts.label: Golgi Apparatus
parts.description: Stacks of flattened sacs that modify, sort and package proteins into vesicles for transport.

parts.name: mitochondria
parts.label: Mitochondria
parts.description: The site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose. Their folded inner membrane (cristae) gives more surface area.

parts.name: eukaryote_ribosomes
parts.label: Ribosomes (Eukaryote)
parts.description: Small structures that build proteins, found free in the cytoplasm or on rough ER.

parts.name: lysosomes
parts.label: Lysosomes
parts.description: Small sacs of digestive enzymes that break down waste, old organelles and invading microbes.

parts.name: vesicles
parts.label: Vesicles
parts.description: Tiny membrane bubbles that carry materials around the cell and to the membrane.

parts.name: centrioles
parts.label: Centrioles
parts.description: A pair of cylinder-shaped structures that help organise the cell during division in animal cells.

parts.name: cytoskeleton
parts.label: Cytoskeleton
parts.description: A network of protein filaments that supports the cell's shape and helps move organelles.

three_d_prompt_drafts.title: Reference Frames, Distance and Displacement
three_d_prompt_drafts.prompt:
1. PURPOSE AND AUDIENCE
An interactive model for middle/early high school physics students. Students should understand that (a) motion is described relative to a chosen reference frame with an origin and axes; (b) position is measured from that origin; (c) distance is the total length of the path actually travelled, a scalar that is never negative; (d) displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, a vector with size and direction, equal to final position minus initial position; and (e) a different reference frame, such as a moving cart, can describe the same motion differently. The scene is a clean tabletop diagram made 3D, not a realistic landscape.

2. OVERALL FORM
A square flat ground board with a grid, about 2 units across, centred at the origin, Z up, top surface at z = 0. Best viewed from above at about 45 degrees from the front-right corner so the winding path, straight arrow and axes are all readable. All markers and arrows sit slightly above the board (z about 0.02 to 0.05) so they never z-fight. Use simple, flat, matte colours.

3. PARTS
`ground_grid` - the reference board; thin box 2 x 2 x 0.04, top at z = 0, light grey with darker grid lines every 0.2 units (model lines as thin raised strips or texture). Background for everything.
`ground_frame_origin` - the origin of the ground frame; small white sphere, radius 0.05, at the back-left corner region (-0.8, -0.6, 0.03).
`x_axis_arrow` - +x axis of the ground frame; red cylinder shaft radius 0.015, length 0.5, with cone tip, from origin pointing +x.
`y_axis_arrow` - +y axis; green, same size, from origin pointing +y.
`z_axis_arrow` - +z axis; blue, same size, from origin pointing up.
`ground_observer` - a person standing still on the ground; simple capsule body plus sphere head, about 0.25 tall, grey-blue, placed just behind the origin at (-0.9, -0.75, 0).
`start_point` - where the object starts; green flat disc/flag post, radius 0.06, at (-0.5, -0.3, 0.02).
`end_point` - where the object finishes; red-and-white checkered or solid red disc with small flag, radius 0.06, at (0.6, 0.2, 0.02).
`path_traveled` - the winding route actually walked; a smooth tube (radius 0.02) following a curve from start_point through about (-0.6, 0.5), (0.0, 0.7), (0.2, -0.3), (0.6, -0.2) to end_point. Orange dashed look (alternating segments) is fine. It must be clearly longer than the straight line.
`distance_tick_marks` - small white rings or beads placed at equal spacing (about every 0.2 units of arc length) along path_traveled, showing distance is counted along the path.
`displacement_vector` - thick straight arrow (shaft radius 0.03, cone head) from start_point directly to end_point, bright purple, raised to z = 0.06 so it floats above the path.
`initial_position_vector` - thin dark-cyan arrow from ground_frame_origin to start_point.
`final_position_vector` - thin dark-magenta arrow from ground_frame_origin to end_point; tip-to-tail with displacement_vector it forms a triangle (initial + displacement = final).
`cart_track` - two thin parallel rails along the front edge at y = -0.85, running x = -0.9 to 0.9, dark grey.
`moving_cart` - a simple box cart 0.35 x 0.2 x 0.1 on four small wheels, yellow, sitting on the track near x = 0.
`cart_frame_axes` - a second, smaller set of axes (length 0.2, same red/green/blue convention but paler) fixed to the cart's top corner, showing the cart's own reference frame.
`cart_observer` - small figure (about 0.2 tall) riding on the cart, light orange, to contrast with ground_observer.
`cart_velocity_arrow` - black arrow beside the cart pointing +x along the track, length 0.35, showing the cart moves relative to the ground.

4. INTERNAL STRUCTURE
No cutaway or transparency needed; everything sits on top of the board and is visible.

5. ACCURACY NOTES
- displacement_vector must be perfectly straight, start exactly at start_point centre and its tip exactly at end_point centre.
- initial_position_vector and final_position_vector both begin exactly at ground_frame_origin; together with displacement_vector they form a closed triangle.
- path_traveled must begin and end at the same two points as the displacement and be visibly longer (roughly 2.5 to 3 times).
- Tick marks are evenly spaced by arc length.
- Axis colours: x red, y green, z blue; axes mutually perpendicular.
- Cart axes move with the cart and are parallel to the ground axes.

6. KEEP IT SIMPLE
No text labels, numbers, scenery, trees, roads or realistic people. No animation required. Use low-poly simple primitives, bright distinguishable colours, and keep each part a separate, clearly named object so students can click it.

parts.name: y_axis_arrow

parts.name: z_axis_arrow

parts.name: ground_observer

parts.name: end_point
